#7769. National Security Division Announces First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.  The company agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.  While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

“This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”

“HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

Pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

Although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

This case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

Please see the Justice Department’s policy here.

#7768. Three Italian Heist Films You Need to See

Ciao ragazzi! Benvenuti! I love Italian cinema, especially from the 1950s and 60s. I’ve been treating myself to the lighthearted crime films of Dino Risi (more on that soon), lately, but I’ve been meaning to rewatch a delightful trifecta of Italian crime comedies starring the beloved star Vittorio Gassman, Italy’s “Il Mattatore” (so-called after a Risi film that he leads). Now that Halloween is over, and we can return to our normal crime programing, I thought we should kick things off Italian-style. Check these out. The first one is genuinely one of the best capers ever made, and the sequels are a lot of fun.

Mario Monicelli directs a crack cast in this wonderful Italian caper which stole my heart. Spoofing Rififi a little bit, it’s a perfect gem of a comedy—Vittorio Gassman plays Giuseppe “Peppe il Pantera” Baiocchi, a petty crook with dreams of being a big-time thief, who plans a perfect pawnshop heist on a quiet block in Rome. But once word gets out about his plot, all manner of unscrupulous characters come out of the woodwork and hope to take part in it. It’s an ensemble cast like you’ve never seen before (hello Marcello!), a phenomenal farce, and an all around fantastico time.

This sequel to Big Deal on Madonna Street sets our favorite band of thieves (still led by Il Mattatore!) after a big-time heist. This time, they have to steal a suitcase of money (containing the pool of bets over soccer tournaments). As you might expect with these guys, though, things don’t go according to plan. Unfortunately, the sequel is not as good as the first, but hey, Claudia Cardinale is in this one!

This sequel to Fiasco in Milan doesn’t live up to the second and definitely doesn’t live up the first, although it does at least attempt to do something new, rather than repeat the success of the first film. In this third chapter, directed by Amanzio Todini, Tiberio (Marcello Mastroianni) is now the main character, fresh out of prison and reuiniting with his old friends from the gang, Peppe (our hero from the last two movies) and Ferribotte.

Olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. Her other work appears in Vanity Fair, Vulture, Lapham's Quarterly, AirMail, the Los Angeles Review of Books, Public Books, The Baffler, Bright Wall/Dark Room, Politics/Letters, The Toast, Truly Adventurous, and elsewhere. She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow. She hosts the podcasst "Culture Schlock" at Lit Hub Radio. She is on instagram at @oldebean, twitter at @oldrutigliano, and bluesky at @oliviarutigliano.bsky.social.

#7767. $5M matching grant moves University of Texas at El Paso closer to opening law school

Heather Wilson (center), the president of the University of Texas at El Paso, speaks at a news conference announcing that the University of Texas at El Paso will soon launch a law school after the Woody and Gayle Hunt Family Foundation pledged a $5 million matching grant. (Photo from the University of Texas at El Paso’s Oct. 28 press release)

The University of Texas at El Paso inched closer to launching a law school after the Woody and Gayle Hunt Family Foundation pledged a $5 million matching grant.

The school’s leaders aim to present the vision for the law school to the Texas legislature in 2027, with the goal of opening in 2030.

In October 2025, the Paul L. Foster Family Foundation also announced a $5 million matching grant, and El Paso, Texas, law firm Tawney, Acosta & Chaparro committed to a $5 million gift in April. Other El Paso firms—including Farah Law, Flores Mendez Law, ScottHulse Attorneys at Law, and Dallas-based Kastl Law—have made donations that will be matched by the Woody and Gayle Hunt Family Foundation’s grant.

The law school would focus on public and private international law involving the United States and Mexico and aims to address the shortage of fluent bilingual lawyers.

#7766. Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.

Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.

“Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

“For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”

“Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States.”

“Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” said Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.”

According to court documents, Lemma held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance. From 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, Lemma conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States.

Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government.

During his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings.

Specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked.

On some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].”

According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. If accepted by the court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. Sentencing is set for April 14, 2027.

The investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office.

The matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division.

#7765. American Woman Convicted of Receiving Military Training from ISIS in Syria

Today, a federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Halima Salman, 27, a U.S. citizen and former resident of Brooklyn, also known as “Umm Khattab al-Muhajir,” of receiving military-type training from the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS), a designated foreign terrorist organization, in Syria. Salman was convicted after a two-week trial before U.S. District Judge Natasha C. Merle.

“The atrocities committed by ISIS, including mass executions, sexual slavery, and the systematic terrorizing of civilian populations, represent some of the gravest crimes of our time,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “There is simply no excuse for aligning with or receiving military training from an organization responsible for such suffering. Today's verdict sends a clear message that those who support this death cult will be found and prosecuted.”

“With today’s verdict, Salman is held accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “ISIS ravaged Syria and caused havoc across the globe; our Office will continue to prosecute those who supported its murderous reign.”

“It’s been nearly a decade since Halima Salman sought military training from ISIS in Syria, and today justice has been served,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI remains unwavering in its vigilance. We will continue to identify, disrupt, and bring to justice those who support foreign terrorist organizations and threaten the safety of our nation and our communities.”

As proven at trial, in September and October 2016, Salman’s parents traveled with her and her eight siblings out of the United States, ultimately destined for ISIS-controlled territory in Syria.

In late 2016 or early 2017, Salman was 18 years old and married to an ISIS fighter in Syria, where she voluntarily sought military-type training and received authorization to carry ammunition and an assault rifle from ISIS. Salman received a document certifying that she successfully completed that training, a copy of which was found on her husband’s cellphone after it was recovered from the battlefield. Also on her husband’s device were photos depicting Salman with an ISIS flag in the background and a video that shows her brandishing an AK-47 rifle.

The case was investigated by the FBI New York Field Office. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs provided significant assistance obtaining evidence overseas.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Adam Amir and Amanda Shami for the Eastern District of New York are prosecuting the case, with valuable assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Reich, Paralegal Specialist Emily Woodruff and Trial Attorney Patrick Cashman of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

#7764. Anna Rasche on the Hope diamond and the trope of cursed jewels in literature

Each year approximately six million people visit the Hall of Minerals in the Smithsonian Museum of Natural History to jostle for a glimpse of the infamous Hope Diamond. Many are afraid to get too close. This singular stone has passed through the hands of adventurers and royalty, heiresses and actresses. And according to legend it brought almost all of them to a bad end.

Today, the Hope epitomizes the “cursed gem.” An object as alluring as it is dangerous; all the wealth of a kingdom, condensed into something that could be forgotten in a coat pocket. But it is hardly alone. Evil jewelry lurks in our earliest mythologies, embeds itself in the pages of history books, and stands at the center of some of our most celebrated works of modern literature.

An early example is the cursed Necklace of Harmonia, wrought by a cuckolded Hephaestus, Greek god of the forge, as a passive-aggressive wedding gift for the daughter born of his wife’s infidelity. Nonnus describes the necklace as a golden tangle of snakes and eagles, encrusted with gems. The tragedies of Oedipus and that of Acteon, who was torn apart by his own hunting dogs, can be traced to this sinister family heirloom.

In India, the Sanskrit texts of the Bhagavata Purana tell of the Syamantaka, a jewel, perhaps a ruby, gifted by the god Surya to the mortal King Satrajit.

The Purana states: “It was the peculiar virtue of that gem, that if worn with all purity it would yield gold and prosperity of the kingdom but if worn by a man of bad character it would bring on his death.”

Indeed, as soon as the stone was in mortal hands it set off a chain of violent deaths. The impure men who possessed it were mauled by a lion, murdered in their sleep, and decapitated. Historians Anita Anand and William Dalrymple hypothesize that the legend of the Syamantaka is the original “curse” legend, one so often attached to important Indian gems.

In the seventeenth century the French gem merchant Jean-Baptiste Tavernier traveled to India, unbothered by any tales of curses. He returned to the court of Louis XIV with spectacular diamonds from the fabled mines of Golconda. One of them would eventually be recut into the Hope diamond. Though Tavernier wrote hundreds of pages about his travels, he never told how he acquired the blue diamond (good business for a gem merchant).

In the absence of a true account, a rumor took hold. It was said that Tavernier prised it from the eye of an idol, invoking a terrible curse. Word spread that he, like Acteon, was eaten by dogs.

What is known for certain is that this blue diamond was stolen during the French Revolution, smuggled into England, and recut to hide its royal French provenance. It reappeared decades later and significantly lighter, in the collection of banker Henry Phillip Hope. Today, most gemologists agree that the missing carats became dust on the cutter’s wheel.

But for a long time it was believed another stone was cut, a blue brilliant of about ten carats. It was said to be owned by the mad Duke of Brunswick, a voracious collector of gems who died exiled from his ancestral seat. The duke’s effects were sold at auction and the blue diamond disappeared. The Brunswick Blue is the mysterious stone, a maybe-sister of the Hope, that inspired the fictional gem called the Midnight in my novel, The Cursed Diamond.

The Hope reemerged in England in the1830s, amid a Gothic Revival where cursed jewels fit right into the zeitgeist. Anne of Geierstein by Sir Walter Scott, published 1829, tells of Lady Hermione, who turned to ash when her precious opal was touched by holy water. (It was Scott’s fiction that launched the still-enduring superstition of opals as unlucky stones). Murky origins aside, the Hope was displayed as a national treasure at London’s Great Exposition of 1851, alongside another Indian diamond with a sinister history.

The Koh-I-Noor, the “mountain of light,” was once a principal treasure of the Mughal Empire. It came into British possession in 1849 after a particularly heartless agent of the British East India Company extorted it from the last Maharaja of the Sikh Empire, the ten-year-old Duleep Singh. The ship that carried the stone to England was plagued by tempests and cholera.

When it was finally presented to Queen Victoria, she accepted it with reluctance, believing it cursed. Luckily for her, an addendum was soon added: the curse only applied to men. To this day the Koh-I-Noor remains in the Crown Jewels of the United Kingdom, a source of contention with India.

Inspired by the Koh-I-Noor, Wilkie Collins invented The Moonstone—the fictional yellow diamond at the center of his 1868 bestselling novel. In this ur-detective novel, a young Englishwoman lands in trouble after inheriting a gem stolen from a Hindu idol by her unsavory soldier uncle. The Moonstone’s success fixed the typical arc of a cursed jewel in the western imagination: illicit origins, greed-induced folly, and bitter ends for those who coveted what was never theirs.

In 1901 Lord Francis Hope sold his family’s blue diamond to cover debts he’d racked up partying his way around the globe with then-wife, American actress May Yohé (Yohé would die in impoverished obscurity, blaming the Hope Diamond for her troubles). For the next eight years the gem passed quietly between dealers and buyers, landing with famed jeweler Pierre Cartier.

Soon, newspapers were cataloguing the misfortunes of the Hope’s previous owners: kingdoms lost, carriages overturned, ships wrecked, heads removed. It is a dark and un-fact-checked history, allegedly encouraged by Cartier to add intrigue and close a sale with American gold heiress Evalyn Walsh McClean and her husband.

After the McCleans purchased the diamond, their lives were marred by tragedy: madness, addiction, political scandal, and accidental deaths. Even so, Evalyn wore the Hope until her death. “Bad luck objects, for me, are lucky,” she said.

The trope of the cursed jewel, a treasure that brings great joy and great sorrow, continues to captivate and inspire works of fiction. It lives in Tolkien’s One Ring. It goes on and on as the Heart of the Ocean in Titanic and burns bright as the Sea of Flames in All the Light We Cannot See. Now, in The Cursed Diamond, it manifests as an icy blue stone called the Midnight, my own humble addition to this enduring lore.

Anna Rasche is a historian and gemologist who has previously worked in the jewelry collection at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and as a curatorial fellow at the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum. Rasche's debut is based on original research she conducted on the uses of gemstones in medieval medicine at the Cooper Hewitt Museum and on site in Italy. She lives in Brooklyn with her husband and infant daughter.

#7763. James Patterson on dictators, historical fiction, and writing a world war II thriller

James Patterson may be one of the world’s most prolific and bestselling authors but there is no secret to his success. It comes down to curiosity and the asking of a simple question that has sustained writers since the beginning of time: What if?

For example: What if, before his rise to absolute power, Adolf Hitler killed his half-niece/mistress Geli Raubal in retaliation for her defiance? And what if he next used his influence over the police and press to have her death declared a suicide? And what if he then waged a campaign of terror against those individuals and institutions who wouldn’t fall in line with that story?

Such speculation served as the impetus for The Munich Affair (Little, Brown and Company; September 21, 2026), a historical thriller based on a true story co-written with frequent collaborator (and “a really wonderful guy”) David Ellis.

“I loved the whole idea. It’s been controversial for a long time,” Patterson says. “I like…taking a real story and then fictionalizing it….We don’t know for sure whether Hitler actually did kill [Geli Raubal].”

The debate is not a new one. Though largely swept under the rug in 1931, a few intrepid reporters—including German activist and journalist Fritz Gerlich—refused to kowtow to political pressure, risking grievous personal and professional reprisals in their search for truth.

“A lot of newspapers chased the story,” Patterson says. “One of them, Fritz Gerlich, wouldn’t give it up…and the reality is that Hitler put Gerlich into Dachau.”

In The Munich Affair, Gerlich—later shot dead at Dachau, the first and longest running Nazi concentration camp in 1934—teams up with (fictional) Detective Thomas Bauer and resistance figure Erich von der Haas in a series of covert operations designed to bring down Hitler’s regime.

Given today’s cultural climate, it’s a markedly timely and topical story for an author who prefers to keep his prose free of politics.

“I don’t talk much about politics,” Patterson says. “But we certainly have a world now, and probably for some time, where we have…dictatorial leaders in several countries.”

And while the authors’ intent wasn’t necessarily to inspire readers to make comparisons between current world leaders and Hitler, perhaps that outcome was inevitable.

“When you read it, you will,” Patterson says. “And I didn’t try to do this, per se…but you do feel some of the things and you go, Hmmm, it sounds like some of the things that are going on now.”

Patterson likens the atmosphere during Hitler’s rise to power and authoritarian rule—in which he was able to declare himself Führer (merging the roles of chancellor and president into one) by manipulating the democratic system and suspending civil liberties—to modern-day aggression, whether North Korea’s totalitarian dictatorship or national operations such as ICE, whose extreme tactics undermine a legitimate issue.

“So, I think [the book] is kind of timely,” he says. “We can think about it and wonder, if to some extent, people blame the Germans for not rising up somehow and overcoming the Nazis…and somehow allowing, or turning a blind eye to, what happened in Germany….”

Which begs the question of whether future generations might reflect on current days with similar retrospect.

“Maybe at some point people will look at this country and ask, ‘Why didn’t we stand up a little bit more and deal with some of the things that are going on now?'” the author says.

Regardless, Patterson maintains that his primary responsibility is to entertain; any education or enlightenment that results is a plus, not the priority.

“You lay out a story, you lay out some information, and you let [the readers] figure it out,” he says. “I’m not a fan of editorializing. I try not to do too much of that.”

Though a departure, the book’s historical context is not unprecedented in Patterson’s wide-ranging oeuvre (which has sold an estimated four hundred and twenty-five million copies worldwide).

It’s something he first experimented with in 2003’s The Jester (co-written with Andrew Gross), in which an innkeeper-turned-pilgrim becomes disillusioned during Europe’s First Crusade and deserts the cause only to devastating consequences.

Like The Jester, The Munich Affair opens with a modern-day prologue, though the book extends this framework to include a secondary storyline in which a contemporary scholar—Eleanor Robbins, a history professor at the University of Chicago—is drawn into the mysteries of the past and travels to Germany to secure evidence of Hitler’s final moments with Raubal.

“In terms of storytelling, it makes it interesting to have her in there, dealing with Neo-Nazis right now,” Patterson says. “You get a feel for a ‘real’ person in the present day…trying to come up with the truth and being in a little bit of danger.”

While her character infuses the narrative with urgency and resonance, Robbins (like Bauer) also underscores the fact that the book is fiction, albeit grounded in the realities of the historical record.

The author recognizes this blurring of the lines for what it is, in contrast to works “masquerading as nonfiction”—such as the hundreds of books written about Shakespeare despite the fact that very little of his life and literary career can be stated with absolute certainty.

For a more comparable example of his intent, Patterson points to Norman Mailer’s anti-Vietnam novel, The Armies of the Night (provocatively subtitled History as a Novel, the Novel as History), which is considered a seminal work in creative nonfiction—a hybrid genre that combines the substance of fact with the style of fiction.

“He would create a lot of scenes and they would be, in his opinion, accurate. But they were still scenes,” Patterson says. “Some people would say, ‘Well, that’s not fair. You can’t do that in non-fiction.’ But he felt you could.”

It’s a similar approach Patterson takes with his own fact-based works, whether fictionalized like The Munich Affair or non-fiction books about tragic figures such as the Kennedys, Marilyn Monroe, and John Lennon or his collaboration with Vicky Ward on a more contemporary crime story, The Idaho Four (and their forthcoming book on Luigi Mangione, American Rage).

“Okay, here’s a scene and obviously I can’t know all the dialogue, but I have a sense of what went on,” he says of his intent to capture the essence of truth. “I think it’s okay as long as you tell people what you’re doing and then they can make their own judgments about it.”

Of course, there are times when creative liberties prevail—particularly when considering the demands of a thriller; such is the case with The Munich Affair’s combustible conclusion.

“We took a lot of license with the ending, but I thought it was…poetic, philosophical. It was an interesting way to pull it all together,” Patterson says. “I think you feel the fiction taking over a bit, but that’s okay, because we’ve had a big dose of [history]….Ultimately, we’re going to get to the bunker.”

Hitler retreated to Berlin’s underground Führerbunker in January 1945, as Allied and Soviet forces began to overtake Nazi strongholds and infiltrate Germany, signaling an imminent end to war.

It’s here that Hitler and his new wife, Eva Braun, died by suicide on April 30. Both ingested cyanide, and Hitler also shot himself in the head with a pistol. Their bodies, once discovered, were then taken to the garden of the Reich Chancellery, where they were set ablaze with petrol for cremation.

Despite official confirmation of this scenario, speculation as to how they died—or even if they died—has persisted to this day. It’s the stuff that conspiracy theories and historical thrillers are made of.

“I don’t think a lot of people are going to guess the ending on this sucker,” James Patterson vows. “They think they know, but they don’t know.”

It’s a promise backed up by decades of writing and hundreds of books, all of which are meant to keep readers turning the pages while asking what next?

John B. Valeri is a book reviewer, author, and host of the web series “Central Booking.” He has contributed to The Big Thrill, CrimeReads, Crimespree Magazine, Criminal Element, Mystery Scene Magazine, The New York Journal of Books, The Strand Magazine, and Suspense Magazine. Visit him online and watch past episodes of “Central Booking” at JohnBValeri.com.

#7761. The best crime novels, mysteries, and thrillers of the month: November 2026

ghbvfgbhvnNovember brings cold winds and chilling adventures, with many of the year’s most intriguing gothics and noirs packed into the month ahead. Most of the following are clear crime and mystery novels; there are two books on the list below that are first-contact thrillers, but I figured their strong X-Files vibes enough to make them count as mysterious.

Thanks to my colleagues Olivia Rutigliano and Dwyer Murphy for their contributions.

Donna Freitas, Wolves of Summer (Soho Crime)

Donna Freitas has already proven herself one of the most fearless and fascinating writers around, especially with the suspense story Her One Regret, which addressed a taboo subject—motherhood, regretted—with compassion, understanding, and nuance. Her newest work, which I devoured in a single day despite the near-500-page length, expands on her previous book’s universe, with a glimpse into character Diana’s first case, as neighbors in a Rhode Island seaside suburb search for a missing girl, and are forced to confront their own long-buried traumas, reemerging in the wake of the preteen’s disappearance. Freitas is particularly concerned with examining the male gaze, the public nature of girlhood, and the terrifying experience of incipient womanhood on the world’s stage. Wolves of Summer should be noted as a mystery of some complexity; craftsmanship shines throughout the novel, and the denouement is perfection. –MO

I haven’t read such a thorough condemnation of such a corrupt little town since Red Harvest. (Almost) everyone in this novel is culpable, although very few of them realize what they are even culpable of, even as the consequences of their actions spiral outwards to the public gaze, and even as the town becomes known nation-wide for both its heinous crimes and its callous attitudes. Harold Rogers sets his tale in Steubenville, Ohio, exploring the lead-up to and and aftermath of a horrific crime, to which the townspeople respond even more horrifically. Rogers’ linguistic prowess and creative talents are on full display here, but never in a way that detracts from understanding the story or its terrible underlying message. A literary tour-de-force, and a noir masterpiece. –MO

Brendan Flaherty, Middleman (Atlantic Crime)

A middle-aged everyman struggling with family life and mounting debts gets drawn into a wild grave-robbing scheme when he moves to a small town with shadowy secrets. Flaherty is a writer on the rise, and his charms are on full display in this new novel, with a story full of big characters with subtly powerful arcs. –DM

Keletso Mopai, We Belong to the Trees (Seven Stories Press)

In immediate post-Apartheid South Africa, a ranch hand is accused of murdering a white farmer, sparking terrible rumors and increasing divisions in their remote township. Mopai uses a kaleidoscopic set of narrators to fill in the gaps and carry the truth forward to a day that can stand to hear it. –MO

Alan Bradley, Numb Were the Beadsman’s Fingers (Bantam)

My heart broke upon hearing of the recent passing of Alan Bradley, the author of the brilliant Flavia de Luce mysteries—not only because I will greatly miss Flavia, but also because I had the chance to meet him personally and discovered him to be as lovely as I could have hoped. Numb Were the Beadsman’s Fingers is his final Flavia novel (his twelfth!), and if ever there were a book to go out on, it’d be this one. It’s about a dead nun, a decades-old case, and a mysterious false identity. RIP to Alan Bradley, and long live Flavia de Luce. –OR

Ian Rankin, The Heights (Grand Central/Cardinal)

Ian Rankin’s stylish, modern take on a very classic mystery premise is a fun addition to November’s literary roster. The story is set in London, in an opulent high rise apartment overlooking Hyde Park. The residents are both impossibly wealthy and glamorous. And when, one night, the nighttime concierge is found dead, they are all suspects. Wheeeee! (This book also has the distinction having a sleuth whose name made me, a silent film fan, do a double-take: Gillian Gish).–OR

This one takes place in the same world as Braking Day, Oyebanji’s mind-bending locked-space thriller of generation ships and factionalism, and functions well as a prequel. Line of Descent asks, what could motivate someone to go so far as to kill amidst the high stakes of disrupting order on a colony ship? Readers might end up surprised, but they will certainly feel satisfied. –MO

Saba Brelvi, The Squatters (The Dial Press)

A well-to-do Muslim woman volunteering at a refuge center strikes up an uneasy connection with two of the migrants interned there, a pregnant woman and her husband, and begins helping them find shelter. After putting them up in a friend’s empty cottage, the woman and her family become the focal point for xenophobic reactionaries in the neighborhood and beyond, even as their connections with their community and their close friends begin to fray irreparably. The Squatters asks essential questions for the present day, and finds no easy answers. What do we owe to our communities, our selves, and our principles? Can a life have meaning without risk? Can words have meaning without subsequent action? And why don’t more books have references to the diggers? Read this shattering work of fiction at your own peril, for you might find yourself, too, standing up for your long-suppressed beliefs no matter the consequences. –MO

Sacha Naspini, The Witch’s Mouth Translated by Clarissa Botsford  (Europa)

Grave robbing in Tuscany from ancient Etruscan graves has been big business since before the war, but with new regulations cracking down on antiquities smuggling elsewhere in Italy, the little band of thieves at the center of the novel face new gangs trying to muscle into their territory, renewed inquiries from weary local authorities, and internal divisions that threaten to dissolve their operation entirely. –MO

Kennedy Cole, There Used to Be People Here (Berkley)

When a queer man dies in a gay bar restroom under, shall we say, unusual circumstances (a giant worm emerges from his mouth and leaves behind the mere husk of a body), two detectives go looking for answers, only to stumble upon a government conspiracy to cover up an alien crash site with deadly cargo. Kennedy Cole uses the language of science fiction to explore the experience of queerness as a person of color; one of the detectives is the first Black policeman in his small southern town, and he’s as drawn to the alien as he is repelled by his colleagues. A moody, atmospheric take on the first encounter thriller, with plenty of body horror thrown in (or perhaps, bursting out). –MO

Molly Odintz is the managing editor for CrimeReads and the editor of Austin Noir, now available from Akashic Books. She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

#7760. Another Trump term?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

President Donald Trump and his policies were a consistent and high-profile theme during the Supreme Court’s last term. The justices weighed in on several of Trump’s signature initiatives, from sweeping global tariffs and his efforts to limit the availability of birthright citizenship to his attempts to fire members of the Federal Trade Commission and Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors – as well as various important immigration cases. And that’s all before you get to the court’s interim docket, where Trump chalked up a number of significant victories.

As it currently stands, the Supreme Court’s 2026-27 term is much less Trump-centric than its predecessor, featuring two challenges to Trump’s immigration policies and a dispute over access to information about Trump’s U.S. Department of Government Efficiency, also known as DOGE. But that could change soon: between Nov. 6 and mid-January, the justices are likely to consider a number of petitions for review filed by the Trump administration or Trump himself. Given the Office of the Solicitor General, which represents the federal government before the Supreme Court, has a high success rate – usually somewhere around 60% – for petitions that it files with the justices, Trump could once again end up dominating the term.

Immigration is already a hot topic on the court’s docket, but two immigration disputes could raise the prominence of the issue even more. When the justices meet for their Nov. 6 conference, one of the cases that they will consider is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, a challenge to a Trump administration policy of quickly removing immigrants who cross the border illegally without giving them the chance to seek asylum.

Two federal courts in Washington, D.C., agreed with the challengers – a group of immigrants and three immigrants’ rights groups – that the policy violates federal immigration law. That prompted U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer to come to the Supreme Court in August, where he argued that the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit “threatens to dismantle” what Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin “describes as an ‘indispensable’ tool for controlling the border.”

Last month, the Trump administration asked the justices to weigh in on another dispute arising from its immigration agenda – this time involving the government’s efforts to detain and deport several students and academics because of their support for Palestine. The government’s petition came in the case of one of those detainees, Badar Khan Suri, an Indian national who came to the United States for a postdoctoral fellowship at Georgetown University. The Trump administration has told the justices that they should also consider granting the petition for review filed recently by Mahmoud Khalil, an Algerian national who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria and became a lawful permanent resident of the United States in 2024. The government contended that both men should be deported based on determinations by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that their conduct – alleged support for the Islamic militant group Hamas, in Suri’s case, and participation in “antisemitic protests and disruptive activities” for Khalil – compromised U.S. foreign policy.

Attorneys for Suri and Khalil went to federal court in New Jersey and Virginia, asking judges there to review the legality of their detentions on the ground that (among other things) they had been detained in retaliation for their speech. As their cases come to the court, the question that the justices have been asked to decide is whether federal trial courts even have the power to consider such challenges, or whether (as the Trump administration argues) those claims are instead barred by federal immigration law, which generally requires all challenges “arising from” deportation proceedings or the decision to begin such proceedings to go first to a federal appeals court, because they are also related to whether one can be deported. The federal courts of appeals have reached conflicting conclusions on the issue, which increases the likelihood that the justices will agree to weigh in.

Suri’s response to the government’s petition for review and the government’s response to Khalil’s petition are both due on Nov. 20. The justices will likely consider both petitions at a private conference sometime early next year.

In June, the Supreme Court granted the federal government’s petition for review in Genalo v. Black, agreeing to address whether there is a point at which a noncitizen has been detained so long that he or she has a constitutional right to a bond hearing and, if so, what standard the government must meet for him or her to remain in detention. That case was scheduled for oral argument in October, but it was dismissed in September because it was moot – that is, no longer a live controversy.

The Trump administration returned to the court later that month, asking the justices to grant a petition for review involving the same questions, which Sauer called “exceptionally important.” The case was filed by a citizen of the Dominican Republic, identified in court filings only as D.C., who has spent most of his adult life in the United States and has three daughters with a U.S. citizen. D.C. was detained on the same day that he finished serving a prison sentence, and the government sought to deport him.

In March 2026, when he had been in immigration custody for almost six-and-a-half months, U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer agreed with D.C. that he was entitled to “an individualized bond hearing, with constitutionally adequate procedural safeguards.” The Trump administration is now appealing that decision to the Supreme Court without waiting for a federal appeals court to rule on the case. Sauer told the justices that “granting immediate review would allow the Court to consider” the questions it had already agreed to decide in Black during the 2026-27 term.

D.C.’s response is currently due on Dec. 8; if that deadline remains in place, the court would likely consider the government’s petition sometime in early to mid-January.

In Trump v. Thakur, the justices will consider a petition for review stemming from the 2025 decision to end research grants from the Environmental Protection Agency, National Science Foundation, and National Endowment for the Humanities for researchers at the University of California. The researchers went to federal court, where they argued that the termination of those grants violated (among other things) their rights to free speech and fair treatment, as well as the federal law governing administrative agencies.

A federal district court issued a preliminary order requiring the government to reinstate the grants. The government went to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which upheld that decision with regard to the claims on the basis that the administration had ended the grants because of the recipients’ “perceived expression of DEI, DEIA, or environmental justice viewpoints.”

The court of appeals rejected the government’s contention that it could terminate funding for programs that, in its view, are not in the public interest. “This overlooks that there is a critical distinction between creating or ceasing a particular program (or subsidy, or forum), on one hand, and discriminating against disfavored speaker viewpoints within a program (or subsidy, or forum), on the other,” the 9th Circuit wrote.

The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court in August, asking the justices to weigh in. Sauer told the court that “if left to stand, the Ninth Circuit’s decision will establish precedent forcing taxpayers to waste countless dollars on private projects promoting ideologies that their public stewards reject.”

Last week Sauer asked the Supreme Court to distribute the government’s petition, as well as the researchers’ brief opposing review, on Oct. 28, without waiting the 14 days normally prescribed by the court’s rules. This would allow the justices to consider the case at their Nov. 13 conference.

In United States v. Jackson, the Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to rule on the legality of Trump’s appointment of an acting U.S. attorney in Nevada. Sauer told the justices that the appointment of Sigal Chattah (as well as others around the country) was not only lawful, but “a critical tool that the Executive Branch has used without meaningful objection for 25 years.”

Under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, the federal law that governs how the executive branch can temporarily staff vacant positions that require presidential appointment and confirmation by the Senate, interim officers can serve for 120 days. Under that law, then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi appointed Chattah as the interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada, effective April 1, 2025, after Jason Frierson, who was nominated by then-President Joe Biden, stepped down.

With only a few days remaining before her interim appointment was set to expire, Chattah resigned, and Bondi designated her as the first assistant U.S. attorney. In that post, Bondi said, Chattah would have the power under the FVRA “to serve as Acting United States Attorney upon a vacancy in that office.” Bondi also gave Chattah the powers of a U.S. attorney for legal proceedings in Nevada.

Three men who had been indicted on felony charges in Nevada after Chattah’s designation as the first assistant U.S. attorney sought to have, at a minimum, Chattah disqualified from appearing in the case as the “Acting U.S. Attorney.” The lower courts agreed that Chattah was not eligible to serve as the acting U.S. attorney, and that she could not play any role in the prosecution of the defendants’ cases.

In a 34-page opinion, Judge Eric Miller of the 9th Circuit wrote that the “text and structure” of the FVRA are “unambiguous: The statute does not permit the executive to fill an existing vacancy by designating a new first assistant.” Instead, he reasoned, the FVRA “provides that a first assistant automatically succeeds to a vacant office” only if the first assistant was first assistant when the principal office became vacant. The automatic-succession rule, he concluded, “does not apply to a first assistant” – like Chattah – “who never served under a validly appointed official.” Moreover, Miller continued, the attorney general cannot achieve the same result “by delegating all of the functions and duties of the U.S. Attorney to someone else.”

In a second petition, United States v. Office of the New York State Attorney General, the Trump administration has appealed a ruling against it by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit in a dispute over the appointment of John Sarcone as the Acting U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of New York. When Sarcone obtained grand jury subpoenas for information from the New York attorney general’s office relating to its investigations of the National Rifle Association and Trump, the office sought to quash the subpoenas on the ground that Sarcone had not been validly appointed.

A federal district court granted that request, and the 2nd Circuit upheld that decision. Sauer came to the Supreme Court in September, where he told the justices that Jackson was a better case in which to consider the validity of Trump’s appointments because the grand jury that issued the subpoenas in the New York case had been discharged and, as a result, the subpoenas were no longer enforceable. He urged the court to hold the New York case until it acts on Jackson.

The defendants challenging Chattah’s appointment have until Nov. 5 to file their brief opposing review; the response of the N.Y. attorney general’s office is currently due on Nov. 2.

There are several other notable petitions pending.

In May 2025, the Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration’s request to temporarily enforce a ban on transgender servicemembers. In a different case just over one year later, a divided panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld part of an order by a federal judge in Washington, D.C., barring the Trump administration from expelling several challengers to the policy from the military. (At the same time, that panel lifted the part of the order that would have required the military to admit transgender people who want to join the armed forces.)

In its petition for review in United States v. Talbott, filed in August, the federal government asked the Supreme Court to review and eventually reverse the D.C. Circuit’s decision. Sauer called it “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”

The response from the challengers is currently due on Nov. 2.

In Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association, the Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on whether and when a federal court can throw out an agency’s action or rule in its entirety – a concept known as “universal vacatur.”

The question comes to the court in a case that began as a pair of challenges (that were later combined) to rules issued to implement parts of a 2022 law that was intended to protect patients from surprise healthcare bills. A federal district court in Texas ruled for the challengers – the Texas Medical Association, a hospital, and four air ambulance companies – but a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit reversed that decision in part.

The case then went to the full 5th Circuit, which threw out some of the challenged provisions. The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court this month, asking the justices to take up the dispute. It pointed to the Supreme Court’s 2025 decision in Trump v. CASA, holding that federal courts do not have the authority to enter so-called universal or nationwide injunctions, which prohibit the government from enforcing a policy anywhere in the country. The same logic underlying that case – the idea that courts “can grant ‘complete relief’ to parties before the court but cannot, as a rule, reach beyond them” – should apply to such regulations, Sauer contended.

The challengers’ response is currently due on Nov. 13, although that deadline may be extended.

Petitions filed by Trump’s personal lawyers

Although the federal government filed all of the petitions discussed above, Trump is also seeking Supreme Court review in three petitions filed by his personal lawyers. The most recent petition is also the one that the justices could consider first: Trump v. Clinton, the president’s bid to revive his lawsuit against Hillary Clinton (and several others, including the Democratic National Committee) alleging “a coordinated scheme … to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion.”

U.S. District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed the lawsuit, finding (among other things) that Trump had brought his claims too late, and that many of the statements alleged to have been made by the various defendants were “plainly protected by the First Amendment.” Middlebrooks also sanctioned Trump and his attorney, Alina Habba, ordering them to pay nearly $1 million.

On appeal, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit largely upheld Middlebrooks’ decision and affirmed the sanctions orders. The full 11th Circuit rejected Trump’s request for reconsideration, prompting Trump – represented by Richard Klugh – to come to the Supreme Court on Oct. 9. He asked the justices to weigh in on two questions: whether the time to file Trump’s claims should have been extended because of his unique role and responsibilities as president, and whether a court can fine the president and his lawyers for making the “substantial, unresolved argument” that the time to file Trump’s claims should have been extended.

Through her longtime attorney, David Kendall, Clinton waived her right to file a response to Trump’s petition. The case has been distributed to the justices for consideration at their Nov. 6 conference. The court is extremely unlikely to grant review without first calling for Clinton to file a brief opposing review.

In Trump v. CNN, the president is seeking to reinstate his defamation case against cable news giant CNN. Trump contends that when CNN used the phrase “the Big Lie” to describe his insistence that he had actually won the 2020 election, which had been stolen from him, it was attempting to link him with Adolf Hitler and Nazi propaganda – which, Trump said, was defamation.

A federal judge in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, dismissed Trump’s case. In an eight-page, unsigned opinion, the 11th Circuit upheld that ruling.

In his petition for review, which was filed in August, Trump contended that “CNN falsely and maliciously portrayed” him “as a knowing liar who fabricated objections to the 2020 election, lacked supporting evidence, and deliberately deceived the American people.”

And in July, Trump filed the second of two petitions arising from lawsuits brought by E. Jean Carroll, who had alleged that in 1996 Trump had sexually abused her in a dressing room at a New York department store. The lawsuit leading to the second petition claimed that in June 2019, Trump had defamed her by calling her a liar – saying, among other things, that Carroll “was trying to sell a new book” and that her accusations were “totally false.” A jury awarded Carroll $83.3 million in January 2024.

The 2nd Circuit upheld the award in 2025, finding “ample evidence that Trump was recklessly indifferent to Carroll’s health and safety” and that “Carroll was subjected to ongoing and prolific harassment as a result of these statements, including a multitude of death threats and other threats of physical injury.” The full court of appeals in April declined to rehear the case.

Represented by a private lawyer, Robert Giuffra, Trump argued in his petition for review that in the wake of the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, in which it held that presidents generally have broad immunity for their acts while in office, the $83.3 million award cannot be allowed to stand. “The threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next,’” Giuffra wrote.

The federal government filed its own petition backing Trump, in which it (like Trump) urged the Supreme Court to also decide whether the court of appeals should have granted then-Attorney General Bondi’s request to recertify that Trump made his statements as part of his role as president and therefore the federal government, rather than Trump, should be the defendant in Carroll’s case.

Carroll’s response to both petitions is currently due on Oct. 30.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

As part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

“No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”

“By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” said U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”

“This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution.  We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”

“The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” said Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”

For nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.

#7756. Karin Slaughter on Mo Hayder, thrillers by women, and the legacy of “Gone”

I clearly remember the first time I read Mo Hayder. Birdman was published in 2000, a year before my own first novel was published, and I felt an intense sense of wonder with every finely crafted sentence. The plotting was fantastic. The characters were not just believable but brought out an array of emotions from lust to disappointment to love to abject fear. The tension knotted more tightly with every turn of the page. I had never read anything like it—and it made me feel more inspired, more challenged, in my own career.

At the time, the genre was a hard place for women. We are supposed to be sugar and spice, the docile victims of these sorts of stories, not the ones who gain control and agency by writing about them with an unblinking eye. That Mo was able to accomplish this, that she broke ground for the many who came behind her, will always be an enduring part of her legacy.

The women who were able to follow, from Gillian Flynn to Ivy Pochoda to Jennifer Hillier, owe a tremendous debt to Mo for helping carve out space in a genre that often celebrates women on the page, but seldom celebrates them the same way in life.

But that’s exactly who Mo Hayder was: a mold-breaker. She was an iconoclast who could not be put in a box, neither as a person nor as a writer. She was bold. Her wit razor sharp. Her humor quirky. She didn’t shy away from writing about very dark things, and that made her an outlier. Her voice on the page was always confident and assured but never bordered into authorial intrusions. She never wrote the same book or told stories the same way twice. Mo Hayder was an icon.

In Birdman, Jack Caffery is a young, driven, seemingly unshockable detective who is faced with the daunting task of hunting down a serial killer who’s leaving behind a trail of horrific crimes—but the story is much more than the plot. Caffery is a character who grabs you by your bones and shakes you into seeing all the darkness in the world. He has messy relationships. He screws up a lot.

But in the end, you’re rooting for him—not just because you want the crime solved but because you want something, anything, to finally go his way. Readers often take it for granted that they will care about a character, but making them care about a character who does unlikable things is the difference between a writer and a master storyteller. Mo certainly deserves that title.

Gone is the fifth book in the Jack Caffery series but it stands very well on its own. By this point, Caffery’s counterpoint, Police Diver & Sergeant Phoebe “Flea” Marley, has been introduced. Marley is a lot like Mo: determined, beautiful, incredibly capable, but not invincible.

Flea and Caffery should have a closer relationship. They would fit together like two puzzle pieces. Unfortunately, they both carry around an awful lot of baggage. While this is tough for them, it makes them come alive on the page. They are excellent counterparts as detectives, and by the end of this novel you’ll be rooting for them both, despite their very deep flaws.

It’s no surprise that Mo won the Edgar® Award for Gone. She takes what already worked so well in this series and pushes up the volume by a thousand. The villain is completely fresh and extremely frightening. The plot takes amazingly satisfying twists that you’ll never see coming. And the story will creep and crawl right under your skin where it will stay forever.

Mo Hayder’s novels are dark, visceral, bold, and brilliant, and she leaves behind a lasting legacy. When she passed away in 2021, the crime writing world was devastated—tributes poured in and readers found solace in her novels—the incredible, brave, important stories she left behind.

Mo was always a writer—and a person—who looked at life as a question to be answered, as shown by her varied career path—not one to simply sit down to write in a vacuum, she made sure she had a wealth of life experience under her belt (she worked as a barmaid, security guard, filmmaker, hostess in a Tokyo club, educational administrator, and a teacher of English as a foreign language, to name but a few). Mo also held an MA in film from The American University in Washington, DC, and an MA in Creative Writing from Bath Spa University.

Writing was her love and her craft, and she took it very seriously. The legacy she leaves behind is not only that of a thriller writer, but of a generous, smart, passionate author and champion of other authors. I remember her as someone who squeezed every ounce out of life and did us all the great kindness of pouring some of that energy into her novels.

Over her many years as a writer, Mo, whose real name is Clare Dunkel, and detective Jack Caffery earned a legion of loyal fans, with Mo’s compulsive stories becoming staples of every crime reader’s bookshelf up and down the country—and indeed, across the globe. The series went from strength to strength, and Mo’s unique writing style and her refusal to shy away from the darker side of life became more and more apparent, setting her apart from other thriller writers and making it impossible for anyone to replicate her.

I am to this day still in awe of her tremendous talent and am deeply saddened that she is gone. We are so lucky that her work lives on.

Introduction by Karin Salughter to Gone by Mo Hayder copyright © 2026 by Karin Slaughter. Reprinted by permission of Grove Atlantic, Inc.

She is the author of more than twenty instant New York Times bestselling novels, including the Edgar-nominated Cop Town and standalone novels The Good Daughter and Pretty Girls. James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, North Carolina, a former U.S. government contractor, was arrested by the FBI on Tuesday for allegedly leaking national defense information by posting the information on a popular social media site, unlawfully retaining other national defense information at his residence, and stealing night vision goggles from the U.S. Army’s Special Operations Command.

Ashbacher was charged by an indictment unsealed Tuesday with unlawfully transmitting and retaining national defense information and with theft of government property.

According to the indictment, beginning in or about 2021, the defendant worked as an employee of a private company that provided security and emergency management services at the U.S. Army Special Operations Command facility in Fort Bragg, North Carolina. To perform the required functions of his employment, Ashbacher held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

As further detailed in the indictment, Ashbacher photographed and removed without authorization videos and photographs containing images of classified military operations and transmitted the materials to a social media site. The classified materials were later re-posted by other users to a second social media site. Ashbacher asked a social media user in a private message to remove some materials and further stated that he was “trying to do some damage control.” A search of Ashbacher’s residence also revealed a classified award write-up that contained additional national defense information, along with a night vision goggle system specific to a military unit within Army Special Operations Command that had been reported missing.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the U.S. Department of the Army’s Criminal Investigative Division.

Trial Attorney Leslie Esbrook of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Logan Liles for the Eastern District of North Carolina are prosecuting the case.

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#7753. How Alain Delon Got Caught Up in a Murder Investigation at the Height of His Fame

The actor lies still. Eyes closed. Waiting for the signal.

‘Silence sur le plateau . . .!’ shouts director Jacques Deray.

The crew falls quiet. A silence descends upon the Saint-Tropez villa. Just the clicking of the cicadas, drunk on the late-summer heat in the scrubland surrounding the azure pool. Thick cables everywhere. Lighting rigs. Flight cases.

‘. . . Moteur . . . Ça tourne . . .’ calls the assistant director.

The camera motors fire up, a soft clicking as the film turning on the reels gets up to speed. The entire crew poised, ready . . .

The camera pans slowly across the glimmering, phosphorescent surface of the swimming pool until, languidly, it finds him: bronzed, lean, 33. Reclined by the water. Dark hair resting on hot sandstone slabs. A glass of orange juice perched on his belly, rising and falling with his breath.

His other hand toys with the water’s surface. Delicately it is withdrawn. Glistening droplets run the length of his fingers and drip sensuously onto his face, revealing to the camera for the first time one of the most famous men in the world.

Not Narcissus, but something colder, l’homme fatal. Nonchalantly, from being mesmerized by the water’s surface and his own reflection, he turns his head towards the sky, raises the glass from his chest and pours the juice into his mouth, slow and sensual.

Dark glasses on. Eyes closed. Pinned to the tiles by the late-summer heat. The remnants of the orange juice drying on his tanned skin.

He is, for now, untouchable. At the height of his powers.

Once the initial observations are complete, the two forensic pathologists begin the next phase of the autopsy. They make a clean incision across the scalp and peel the skin down on either side, revealing the smashed cranium beneath. The top of the skull is sawn off, the brain removed. Next, they open the torso, slicing through the abdomen to extract the vital organs. No major anomalies, except the liver. Enlarged, discoloured. Consistent with long-term alcohol abuse.

Once the examination is complete, the organs, including the brain, are placed back in the body cavity. The skull is reassembled; the skin pulled back into place and stitched at the crown. Fingerprints are taken and sent to the central police archives in Paris. The man still has no name.

Based on decomposition, the doctors estimate the time of death to be a week earlier, most likely during the night of 22 to 23 September. In their report, they write plainly: the skull had ‘completely collapsed in’. Cause of death: blunt force trauma to the head with a heavy object. The theory holds – for now – that it was a fight, something that got out of hand.

They sign the paperwork. The report is dispatched to the investigating judge.

Patard reads the autopsy report and gives the photographs a cursory glance. He can’t place it, but something feels off.

It’s the hands that catch his eye. Everyone insists the victim is a vagabond. But how many vagabonds have manicured nails?

The next day, a fingerprint match comes through. The deceased is one Stevan Markovic. Thirty-one years old. Born in Belgrade, 1937. The same prints first appear on records in 1958, when this man applied for political asylum in Paris. Then again:

Prison in Chambéry, 1962 La Santé, Paris, 1965 Namur, Belgium, 1964 Annecy, 1967

His last registered address? 22 Avenue de Messine, in the prestigious 8th arrondissement on the Rive Droite. A stone’s throw and the quartier of the Elysée Palace.

Then another twist. When cross-referenced, it would appear that 22 Avenue de Messine is also home to a famous actor: Alain Delon.

A file arrives from the Brigade Mondaine – the Paris vice squad. Technically tasked with investigating moral crimes, the Mondaine is unofficially tasked with monitoring the rich.

Patard flicks through their dossier on Delon, it’s only a few pages long; a couple of minor run-ins with the law. But then there are the photos: Delon with known gangsters, Corsicans, men who once fought for the Resistance and now run rackets out of Pigalle or control the ports in Marseille.

Who exactly is this Delon? Patard wonders. He calls in two detectives. ‘Go to Avenue de Messine,’ he says. ‘Interview Delon. Find out who this man was to him.’

The detectives stand there, open-mouthed.

‘Right,’ Patard says. ‘Let me know what you find.’

Patard glances at the paperwork again. The residency permit lists the dead man as a political refugee. Occupation: doublure – a stand-in. A stand-in, it would seem, for Alain Delon.

Unlike the two detectives, Patard isn’t impressed. He’s never seen a Delon film. Doesn’t plan to. But something tells him – this case is about to get complicated.

Edward Chisholm, author of A Waiter in Paris, was born in England and moved to Paris after graduating from the School of Oriental and African Studies in London. His work has appeared in The New York Times, The Guardian, and The Financial Times magazine. He lives in England.

#7751. Judge advances McDonald’s McRib lawsuit that alleges deceptive marketing

A federal judge in Illinois on Friday did not dismiss a proposed class action lawsuit accusing McDonald’s McRib of misleading customers about the sandwich’s ingredients. (Photo from Getty Images)

A federal judge in Illinois on Friday did not dismiss a proposed class action lawsuit accusing McDonald’s McRib of misleading customers about the sandwich’s ingredients.

The plaintiffs allege that the McRib, which costs $7, is shaped to look like ribs and misleads customers in ads to think that it contains rib meat instead of cheaper pork cuts.

In Chicago, U.S. District Judge April Perry of the Northern District of Illinois dismissed some claims, but she did not accept the McDonald’s argument that a reasonable customer could expect the McRib to contain rib meat. Perry said ads of the rib-shaped patties could possibly be an attempt to defraud, but more proof was needed, according to coverage by Reuters.

“Plaintiffs’ proffered understanding of ‘McRib’ is not unreasonable or fanciful,” Perry wrote.

McDonald’s contends that it does not use hearts, tripe or stomach as McRib ingredients, which the suit alleges. The fast-food giant, which has sold the sandwich since 1981, said distinctive product names do not fool reasonable consumers.

“This lawsuit distorts the facts, and ⁠the claims are meritless,” McDonald’s said in a statement.
