#7749. The Trump administration’s attempt to prevent noncitizen voting and the role of the Supreme Court

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court may soon see another clash between the original public meaning of the Constitution and President Donald Trump’s wishes. The birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is one previous example of this. The next instance, which looms on the horizon, involves the issue of noncitizen voting.

The Trump administration has been aggressively undertaking efforts to get states to take steps aimed at preventing noncitizens from voting. The latest such effort is a lawsuit that Trump’s DOJ has filed against California seeking to force the state’s election officials to segregate mailed ballots cast by anyone on a list of 20,000 registered voters whom the Trump administration believes to be noncitizens. As of this writing, the suit is pending in the federal district court, after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit denied DOJ’s emergency appeal for failing to give the district court an adequate chance to issue a ruling, but the merits of the case are likely to make their way to the Supreme Court very soon.

As authority for its suit against California, Trump’s DOJ is relying upon the federal statute that makes voting by noncitizens in federal elections a crime: 18 U.S.C. § 611. There are two fundamental problems, however, with DOJ’s reliance on this statute. First, the original public meaning of the Constitution does not give Congress the authority to make voting by noncitizens a crime; rather, the Constitution leaves it to the states to decide whether or not noncitizens may vote, and this is true even for federal elections.

Second, even assuming that 18 U.S.C. § 611 is a valid exercise of congressional power under the Constitution, it does not authorize DOJ to seek an injunction that would interfere with a state’s rules and procedures for conducting the “manner” of the current congressional elections. Article I, Section 4 of the Constitution provides that state law will govern the “manner” of administering congressional elections unless and until Congress enacts alternative procedures for their administration; 18 U.S.C. § 611 is a criminal law and does not regulate the “manner” of administering elections and thus offers no basis for DOJ or a federal court to supersede the state’s administration of the election.

As to the first problem, the Constitution creates a clear division of authority between determining who can vote in congressional elections and regulating how the voting process occurs. As to the how, as noted, Article I, Section 4 of the Constitution empowers Congress to override state regulations if Congress so wishes. But as to the who, the Constitution lodges the power to determine the qualifications for voting in congressional elections to the states, with Congress having no authority to change those qualifications.

To be sure, a series of important constitutional amendments constrains the degree to which states can set those qualifications. The 15th Amendment prohibits racial discrimination in doing so. The 19th Amendment similarly prohibits sex discrimination with respect to voting rights. The 24th Amendment prohibits a state from making payment of a poll tax a qualification for voting in a federal election. And the 26th Amendment prohibits states from denying an equal opportunity to vote based on age to any citizen at least 18 years old.

But none of these amendments prevent states from setting other qualifications or extending the right to vote. States, for example, could grant 16-year-old citizens the right to vote in congressional elections, and Congress cannot override a state’s decision to do this. The Constitution is explicit on this point. Article I, Section 2, clause 1 provides for the House of Representatives that “the Electors in each State shall have the Qualifications requisite for Electors of the most numerous Branch of the State Legislature.” The 17th Amendment contains the same provision for elections to the U.S. Senate. Thus, if a state were to grant 16-year-old citizens the right to vote for the lower house of the state legislature, the Constitution requires that 16-year-old citizens in that state must have the right to vote for that state’s Representatives and Senators in Congress. No Act of Congress could take away this right to vote in congressional elections granted to 16-year-olds by the state.

The same point applies to voting by noncitizens. Currently, no state chooses to let noncitizens vote for the lower house of the state’s legislature. But if a state decided to let resident aliens vote in these elections, then resident aliens would also be eligible to vote in the state’s congressional elections.

The Supreme Court previously has made clear this distinction between who and how. In 2013’s Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Arizona, Inc., which involved the National Voter Registration Act, Justice Antonin Scalia wrote in the opinion for the court (with its own emphasis on the two key words): “Arizona is correct that the Elections Clause empowers Congress to regulate how federal elections are held, but not who may vote in them.” Scalia elaborated: “Prescribing voting qualifications, therefore, ‘forms no part of the power to be conferred upon the national government’ by the Elections Clause, which is ‘expressly restricted to the regulation of the times, the places, and the manner of elections’” (quoting Alexander Hamilton in The Federalist No. 60). Scalia then explained why: “This allocation of authority sprang from the Framers’ aversion to concentrated power. A Congress empowered to regulate the qualifications of its own electorate, Madison warned, could ‘by degrees subvert the Constitution.’”

The prohibition on noncitizen voting in 18 U.S.C. § 611 contravenes this constitutional division of authority. This congressional statute makes it “unlawful for any alien to vote in any election held solely or in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for … Member of the Senate [or] Member of the House of Representatives,” and it does so regardless of whether the state in question permits noncitizens to vote in these elections. The statute lets states allow noncitizens to vote for state or local offices, but a state must do so “in such a manner that an alien has the opportunity to vote for such other purpose, but not an opportunity to vote for a candidate for any one or more of such Federal offices.” Thus, according to this federal statute, a state has no choice in the matter of whether or not a noncitizen can vote in a congressional election. This makes 18 U.S.C. § 611 unconstitutional.

I am not the first to reach this conclusion. A federal district court in Florida did so recently. More significantly, that district court had asked Paul Clement, the distinguished former U.S. solicitor general in President George W. Bush’s administration, to write an amicus brief on the issue. After undertaking a thorough analysis of the matter, Clement concluded “the better view is that because §611 was intended to criminalize alien suffrage in federal elections, regardless of state law, it sets a voter qualification—which only the states may do.”

To be clear, Congress can make noncitizen voting a crime if (but only if) that criminality is contingent on noncitizen voting also being unlawful in the applicable state. In that context, the congressional statute could be understood as merely regulating procedures for implementing congressional elections, and not determining who is permitted to vote in them. One might then try to argue that 18 U.S.C. § 611 can be sustained as this kind of statute as long as the relevant state currently criminalizes noncitizen voting. The difficulty with this argument, as Clement explained, is that § 611 is not written that way; instead, it emphatically makes noncitizen voting in congressional elections a federal crime regardless of what the state wants.

In any event, let’s assume that 18 U.S.C § 611 could be construed to be constitutional in the way just described. That still doesn’t give Trump’s DOJ the authority to seek an injunction in federal court to force California to change its procedures for administering the current congressional election. Congress would have needed to enact a different law, exercising its authority under the Constitution’s Article I, Section 4 to “alter” the “manner” by which California has chosen to regulate the voting process.

There was a time in American history when Congress enacted a statute to provide federal oversight of a state’s procedures for conducting congressional elections. In the wake of the Civil War, the first Enforcement Act of 1871 empowered two federal “supervisors” in each of the state’s voting precincts, who were appointed from “different political parties” by the federal circuit court for their state, to monitor the voting process for congressional elections. This statute gave these supervisors authority similar to what Trump’s DOJ is currently seeking. The supervisors, for example, could “challenge any vote offered by any person whose legal qualifications the supervisors, or either of them, shall doubt.” To be sure, these supervisors were not part of the Department of Justice, which Congress had created the previous year. Rather, the requirement that these two supervisors be from “different political parties” and appointed by the judiciary was designed to keep them insulated from a cabinet department under the control of a partisan president.

In any event, in 1894 Congress repealed all the provisions of the 1871 Act that had created these supervisors for congressional elections. Nothing like them existed until the Voting Rights Act of 1965, when Congress enacted new provisions for monitoring elections and enforcing the prohibition against racial discrimination in voting. These new provisions did give some significant enforcement powers to the DOJ and federal courts, but they were focused on guaranteeing the equal opportunity to vote regardless of race. These new provisions did not give DOJ or the federal courts any authority to interfere with the counting of ballots in a congressional election in order to prevent ballots cast by noncitizens from being counted.

Indeed, throughout the 20th century, the prevailing understanding was that federal courts lacked the power to intervene in a state’s procedures for counting votes in a congressional election, even if a suit was brought by a candidate with a direct stake in the matter. The most famous example of this is the 1948 Senate race that Lyndon Johnson won by 87 votes. His opponent, former Texas governor Coke Stevenson, sued in federal court to block the counting of votes believed to be fraudulent in the infamous Ballot Box 13. In an exercise of the Supreme Court’s emergency docket, however, Justice Hugo Black ordered that the federal court refrain from interfering with the state’s counting process. After an unusual four-hour oral argument held in Black’s chambers, which he permitted members of the press to attend, he announced his ruling orally. The New York Times reported that he stated that “before a court interfered with an election there must be a statute clearly authorizing this.” The Times also quoted Black as saying, “I think it is impossible to interpret present statutes that Federal courts may go into a state and suspend its process of electing a Senator.” (For more details on the fight over Ballot Box 13, see chapter 8 of my 2024 book “Ballot Battles: The History of Disputed Elections in the United States.”)

There is one caveat. In Bush v. Gore, the court modified Black’s understanding of the federal judiciary’s power insofar as that unusual (and controversial) case permitted a candidate to assert an equal protection claim as grounds for constraining a state’s election procedures. But Bush v. Gore did not involve a suit by the federal DOJ. Indeed, President Bill Clinton insisted that his administration refrain from any involvement in the litigation between the two candidates in the 2000 presidential election. The idea that the federal DOJ could have brought suit in federal court to control the counting process in that election – contrary to Florida’s own procedures – would have astonished even those who supported the idea that the candidates themselves could invoke the authority of the federal courts to enforce Florida’s compliance with constitutional requirements respecting the electoral process.

The bottom line is this: In a congressional election, the state administers the electoral process according to its own laws, subject to the prerogative granted to each congressional chamber by Article I, Section 5 to be the “Judge of the Election … of its own Members.” If Congress wants to add DOJ-initiated federal court proceedings to the overall process of counting, canvassing, and certifying the votes in a congressional election – which would still be subject to being overridden by the ultimate authority of each chamber to adjudicate any disputes over the outcome pursuant to Article I, Section 5 – Congress can do by exercising its Article I, Section 4 authority. But unless and until Congress does that, DOJ has no role to play.

Trump and his DOJ clearly wish the situation were different. But it is the job of the Supreme Court to uphold the law as it is. That job may require the court to reject the effort by Trump’s DOJ to interfere with California’s procedures for conducting this year’s midterm elections.

Edward B. (Ned) Foley holds the Ebersold Chair in Constitutional Law at The Ohio State University, where he also directs its Election Law program.

#7747. Bobcats, “Twin Peaks,” deer: What influenced Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes’ new novel

I love and often teach the memoir People Who Led to My Plays by Adrienne Kennedy. In the book, Kennedy lists all the diverse people, objects, works of art, images, songs, and events that shaped her as an artist. The result is a portrait of a singular artist, a time period, and a manual for becoming an artist.

I have borrowed her form here to explore some of my influences.

Many years ago, my parents sent me a video of a female bobcat being released in the woods outside their home in Northern Wisconsin. It was deep winter, the snow several feet high. An acquaintance of theirs had trapped the bobcat to stop it from terrorizing his neighbor’s chickens and he felt my parents’ woods was a safe place to release her. This news alone would have been interesting enough, but the specifics of the video fascinated me.

The bobcat snarled in the cage, her fluffy winter coat standing on edge, looking both surprisingly small and terrifyingly dangerous. Her captor placed a frozen duck carcass on the snow outside the cage, opened the door, and quickly backed away. But the bobcat didn’t move. She stayed in the cage. The door was open, yet she stayed.

That image captivated me and I started building a story and characters around it.

In my twenties, everyone in my friend group loved Twin Peaks. But I hated it. It frightened me, on many levels, and I hated the way Laura Palmer’s dead and aestheticized body was used to create a story around, a story she had no say in. I wanted to examine this trope of the “beautiful dead girl”: to see if I could write about the real danger women and girls face without making them a spectacle, to see if there was a way to give them agency in a culture that took so much from them.

“—But I love/ life/ I get to be/ in it/ From somewhere else/ in the world/ I am living….”

I consumed all seven episodes ravenously and in quick succession, in the days when I could stay up all night watching TV, letting the images soak into my mind in the thin, vulnerable hours of early morning. I loved the misty forests and the character of the deep, dark lake, the isolation and strangeness. Though the story takes place in New Zealand, the setting felt very similar to places I’d known in Wisconsin. And the missing girl takes action, shapes the story, has a life after the crime that incites the series.

I’d heard and read this folktale, of a mysterious woman completely covered in hair who haunts the jungles of the Caribbean. Her backwards feet confuse those who’d try to track her and her name means “so beautiful” despite or in spite of her sometimes-vengeful nature and her unabashed wildness.

When I saw paintings of her by Firelei Baez—her hair intricately painted fur, her body melding with palms and fauna, her backward feet sprouting kitten heels—the ciguapa began haunting me, stalking in and around my novel.

My family, like countless others, has been irrevocably shaped by the opioid crisis. I carried, and still carry, rage against the Sackler family and others whose criminal and greedy actions caused so much pain and suffering. I wanted to punish them. I wanted to indict them. But I write novels and I didn’t want to write a novel about them. Instead, Clear Water was a way of transforming that rage, of telling the stories of the victims and survivors of this crisis.

In Wisconsin, deer are everywhere. They are full of contradictions: both sustenance and a nuisance—carrying disease, eating flowers and vegetables, totaling cars. They can be both prey and cause destruction. They can seem almost tame, yet are dangerous to approach. They are common and graceful. These contradictions became an intricate part of my book—deer acting as both symbols and forces of their own in the narrative.

Stephen Graham Jones has written many fabulous books since Ledfeather in 2008, but I read this novel at a pivotal moment in the writing of Clear Water. The way Jones interweaves different timelines, the way history shapes the present, and the relationships between humans and animals served as a North Star for my own writing.

I listened to her early albums on repeat while writing Clear Water. Her songs look without faltering at the pain of poverty, violence, and loss yet remain so tender, so full of love and hope.

The forests and lakes of Wisconsin are both the setting of Clear Water and forces that shape the story and the characters. Oaks drop acorns that messages could be carved on. Pines are the only green visible for months in the winter. Birch roots hold the land together. Leaves and pinecones and acorns drop into the lakes, dyeing the water a deep brown tinged with orange.

Even shallow water is opaque. Many beings seek refuge there. Anything could hide there.

Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes is the author of The Sleeping World, Clear Water, and Are We Ever Our Own. She has received fellowships from Hedgebrook, Willapa Bay Artists in Residency, Yaddo, the Millay Colony, Lighthouse Works, and the Blue Mountain Center. She holds a BA from Brown University, an MFA from the University of Colorado, Boulder, and a PhD from the University of Georgia. She is an associate professor at the University of Maryland. She lives in Maryland with her family.

#7746. Assessing the first round of oral arguments of the 2026-27 term

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson – typically the court’s most frequent speaker at oral argument – began the term relatively quietly. In Suncor Energy v. Boulder County, the first argued case, she spoke the fourth-most among the participating justices, accounting for only 12.1% of the court’s words. But that relative silence did not last. Jackson led three of the next four arguments and finished the six-case sitting with 6,254 words, significantly more than any of her colleagues.

The arguments produced other patterns, some less predictable. Jackson and Justice Sonia Sotomayor repeatedly concentrated their attention on the same litigating side, but Justice Neil Gorsuch did so as well, despite the justices’ ideological differences. At the same time, their questions did not necessarily point toward identical legal outcomes.

The cases themselves – and how they were treated – revealed something more. Disputes concerning climate litigation, veterans’ constitutional claims, retirement-plan investments, and environmental review all raised questions about when, where, and under what conditions judicial intervention is available. Indeed, that essentially became the theme of the court’s October session.

Jackson’s dominance and some unexpected cross-ideological alignment

As described above, Jackson’s relatively limited involvement in Suncor initially appeared to vary from one of the Supreme Court’s most consistent recent patterns. During the 2025-26 term, she accounted for 22% of justices’ total speech and led in 41 of 58 oral arguments. Yet in the first argument of this term, her 829 words represented only 12.1% of substantive justice speech, placing her fourth among eight participating justices. Across the other five arguments, however, Jackson’s share averaged 21.0%. By the end of the sitting, Jackson had spoken 6,254 words, more than any colleague, and accounted for 19.3% of all substantive justice speech.

Jackson’s questioning also revealed a recurring alignment with Sotomayor and, more surprisingly, Gorsuch. Across several disputes, the three justices repeatedly directed a disproportionate amount of attention toward the same side.

In Johnson v. United States Congress, for instance, Gorsuch questioned whether the veterans’ benefits system possessed the competence to adjudicate constitutional challenges, while Sotomayor emphasized the burden of forcing veterans through an administrative process prior to obtaining constitutional review. Jackson similarly challenged the government’s account of how constitutional questions were handled in practice. The three justices’ approaches differed, but all three explored weaknesses in the government’s proposed review scheme.

In Suncor, the justices’ shared focus covered up larger doctrinal disagreements. Jackson questioned whether the case was sufficiently developed for Supreme Court intervention. Sotomayor asked about the courts’ authority and whether specific arguments had been preserved. Gorsuch explored how the Clean Air Act affected federal common law and potential state-law restrictions.

These alignments should not be conflated with emerging voting coalitions, however. In Beaird v. United States, for example, a Federal Sentencing Guidelines case, Jackson and Gorsuch proved the argument’s two dominant speakers while developing substantially different accounts of the U.S. Sentencing Commission’s authority.

The lesson is this: The justices who identify pressure points in an argument do not always group along familiar ideological lines, and agreement about which position deserves examination need not produce agreement about the possible controlling rule.

Jackson’s individual prominence did not translate into liberal dominance of the court’s collective conversation. Across the six arguments, conservative justices contributed 54.3% of substantive justice speech, compared with 45.7% from the three liberals. Conservatives supplied the majority of justices’ words in five of the six cases, with Johnson the exception. This represents a somewhat different balance (so far) from the 50.9% conservative–49.1% liberal division reported in a previous Legalytics analysis of the 2025-26 term.

Perhaps more revealing was the distribution of participation within those blocs. Justice Brett Kavanaugh finished second across the sitting with 5,031 words, followed closely by Justice Elena Kagan (4,998) and Gorsuch (4,920). Yet the three justices occupied markedly different positions from argument to argument. Kavanaugh supplied 23.7% of the justice’ speech in Suncor but only 6.0% in Johnson. Gorsuch ranged from 25.7% in Beaird to just 1.2% in Salazar v. Paramount Global. Kagan, who averaged 21.2% across the opening-day arguments, averaged only 13.6% across the next four.

Overall, the six arguments revealed neither the conservative or liberal bloc dominating the conversation. Instead, participation shifted substantially with the legal questions presented, often placing different justices at the forefront of particular disputes. Those changes become especially consequential when examining the competing theories of judicial review and interpretive authority developed throughout the individual arguments.

Four arguments about access to judicial review

Four of the court’s first six arguments presented different versions of a recurring question: what must happen before a federal court can intervene in a case? The doctrines varied considerably, from Supreme Court jurisdiction and veterans’ constitutional claims to pleading requirements and administrative finality. Nevertheless, each argument required the justices to consider how procedural and institutional/justiciable boundaries determine whether a legal challenge can proceed.

The sharpest illustration came in Department of the Air Force v. Prutehi Guåhan, where the justices examined whether the Air Force’s decision to seek a territorial hazardous-waste permit constituted final federal agency action, and how that determination interacted with environmental review under a federal statute. The government received 67% of explicit question marks but accounted for only 52.7% of advocate speech. Its counsel, Sopan Joshi, experienced a 60% cutoff rate, which was the highest among the 15 advocates appearing during the sitting.

The exchanges revealed different understandings of when an agency decision is settled enough to justify judicial intervention. Kagan questioned whether an agency’s completed deliberations could be rendered non-final simply because another regulator’s approval remained necessary. Jackson, typically on Kagan’s side, focused on the opposite possibility: if Guam’s permitting authority could impose conditions materially changing the Air Force’s project, perhaps the application remained a proposal rather than an operative federal commitment. Justices Clarence Thomas and Amy Coney Barrett called out the unusual institutional arrangement, with the federal government appearing as a regulated applicant rather than the permitting authority itself.

Gorsuch and Chief Justice John Roberts approached the problem from another angle, exploring whether postponing review could leave challengers without an effective opportunity to challengee the federal government’s environmental obligations. Kavanaugh explored the practical consequences of requiring successive rounds of review.

The relationship to the opening-day cases is telling. In Suncor, Thomas and Jackson questioned whether the dispute was sufficiently developed for Supreme Court review, particularly with other federal issues and several factual questions still unresolved below. In Johnson, the justices confronted a very different institutional barrier: whether constitutional challenges involving veterans’ benefits must proceed through the specialized administrative-review system rather than federal district court. Jackson, Sotomayor, and Gorsuch each tested aspects of the government’s proposed route, including whether it provided a practical means of resolving constitutional claims.

Anderson v. Intel Corporation Investment Policy Committee brought up a related yet distinct procedural issue. There, the question was what a retirement-plan plaintiff must allege to advance a claim that an ERISA fiduciary failed to use the requisite “care, skill, prudence, or diligence” under certain circumstances. Kavanaugh and Jackson distinguished underperforming investments from allegedly imprudent asset-allocation strategies, while Kagan and Barrett examined how rigorous a “meaningful investment benchmark” must be.

These cases do not rest on a particular judicial ideology. But they all deal with the availability of judicial review: whether the litigation has reached a proper point, the question of an adequate forum, the sufficiency of the allegations, and whether the court’s intervention is appropriate yet.

Beaird: competing theories of legal authority

No argument during the sitting generated more speech from the justices than Beaird v. United States. The justices contributed 7,791 words, more than twice their total in Anderson, with Gorsuch and Jackson accounting for 25.7% and 22.4% of these, respectively. Together, the two justices provided nearly half the court’s substantive speech. Yet their exchanges revealed a profound difference in how they understood the authority of the U.S. Sentencing Commission and the legal status of its commentary.

The dispute asks whether Stinson v. United States, the court’s 1993 decision requiring deference to Sentencing Guidelines commentary under specified conditions, continues to supply the governing rule. The case’s unusual alignment further distinguished the argument. Both Beaird and the United States supported vacating the judgment, and the court thus appointed a “friend of the court,” Anthony Dick, to defend Stinson. The petitioner-aligned advocates consequently accounted for 68.3% of advocate speech and received 80.1% of justice words. This imbalance partly reflects the unusual distribution of advocates rather than necessarily indicating hostility toward their position.

Jackson, who once served on the Sentencing Commission, began by challenging the premise that the Sentencing Guidelines and their commentary can meaningfully be separated. In her account, sentencing judges rely on both parts of the Guidelines Manual to calculate the recommended sentencing range. Commentary helps determine how provisions operate together as opposed to consisting of an unrelated agency interpretation. She returned to Congress’ decision to establish a sentencing framework intended to limit disparities among similarly situated defendants, questioning whether importing limitations from administrative deference doctrine would undermine that design.

Gorsuch’s questioning approached the problem from a very different institutional perspective. He examined where Congress expressly authorized binding commentary, why the Commission should be able to accomplish through commentary what it could instead accomplish through formal Guidelines amendments, and whether deference would weaken the procedural safeguards associated with that process. His concerns extended to the incentives created by allowing the Commission to make authoritative interpretations without necessarily following the same procedures applicable to the Guidelines themselves.

Other justices explored possible consequences of either approach. Kavanaugh repeatedly returned to the stability of a system operating under Stinson for more than three decades, questioning whether revisiting the doctrine might introduce new uncertainty into sentencing. Kagan examined whether Congress’ express recognition of policy statements complicated efforts to distinguish them from commentary, suggesting that differences in terminology might not fully resolve the question of authority.

The exchanges suggest several possible routes to a decision: reaffirming the current system, limiting the circumstances under which commentary receives controlling weight, or requiring a more explicit statutory basis for binding interpretations. They also illustrate a theme from earlier research on the relationship between oral argument and eventual opinions: The most revealing material may not be which advocate received the most questions, but the competing legal frameworks the justices developed as they questioned counsel.

The first six arguments also revealed substantial differences in how advocates were able to develop their answers. Across 982 advocate speaking turns, 420 ended in an explicitly identifiable cutoff by a justice, a rate of 42.8%. That figure was somewhat higher on the first day (45.2%) than during the four subsequent arguments (41.4%), but the variation among individual advocates was significantly larger.

Joshi, representing the Air Force in Prutehi, experienced the sitting’s highest cutoff rate at 60.0%, with 66 of his 110 turns ending that way. Kannon Shanmugam followed at 56.9% in Suncor, while Paul Clement was at 55.2% in Salazar. These were not merely differences between government and private counsel but arose in disputes involving separate statutes, procedural issues, and judicial argument coalitions.

Even advocates supporting the same position had different experiences. In Suncor, Shanmugam’s median response was 13.5 words, compared with 35 for Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris, who supported the petitioner and experienced a 40.0% cutoff rate.

The differences illustrate how much the structure and subject of individual exchanges can shape an advocate’s opportunity to explain a legal position. These observations also complement earlier Empirical SCOTUS findings about an increasingly active oral-argument bench.

Jackson’s unusually limited participation in the first argument of the term, Suncor, proved to be an exception rather than the beginning of a broader retreat. Across six arguments, she remained the court’s leading individual speaker, even as the distribution of judicial participation shifted considerably from case to case.

More surprising was the relationship between the justices’ attention and their ideological positions. Jackson, Sotomayor, and Gorsuch consistently concentrated on the same litigating side. But their exchanges also revealed why common questioning should not be confused with voting the same. In Beaird, for example, Jackson and Gorsuch developed competing accounts of institutional authority despite both dominating the argument.

The substantive disputes supplied another connection. From Suncor and Johnson to Anderson and Prutehi, the justices repeatedly considered when judicial review should be available. Despite some of the substantive issues in play, the defining theme of this term’s start was one of judicial power.

Dr. Adam Feldman is the creator and author of the blog Empirical SCOTUS and the Substack Legalytics.

#7745. Wole Talabi on the intersection of first contact stories and mysteries

In 1985, just a few weeks after a bloodless coup during which Major-General Ibrahim Babangida overthrew the military government of Major General Muhammadu Buhari in Nigeria, American astronomer Carl Sagan published Contact. A novel in which humanity first encounters advanced extraterrestrial intelligence when a team of scientists at SETI (Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence) detects a radio signal from the star system Vega, located twenty-six light years away containing a sequence of prime numbers.

As they investigate, they uncover an embedded video and instructions in binary for building a mysterious interstellar Machine. Nations unite to fund and construct the device and a small international crew travel through the machine to meet the alien intelligence near the center of the galaxy where the aliens reveal their grand cosmic plans. It’s a great story.

First Contact narratives like Contact are some of my favorite stories in all of science fiction. As a species, we’ve long wondered about our place in the universe: if we were alone in it and if not, what would it be like to encounter alien intelligence.

Ever since I was a boy growing up under military dictatorship in Nigeria, discussing current affairs, history and astronomy with my dad on the weekends, I have found it endlessly fascinating to imagine all the different ways that a first encounter between humans and extraterrestrial sapient life could go. So of course, I enjoyed reading Contact when I found it in my school library and especially loved watching the 1997 screen adaptation starring Jodie Foster.

Readers often think of First Contact stories like Contact, and the many others that came before and after, as being focused on scientific or philosophical discovery, but undergirding all the talk of orbital mechanics, biology, astronomy, communications protocols and alien artifacts are much simpler things: questions.

First Contact stories are about answering questions. That, I think, is exactly what makes most First Contact stories at their core, mystery stories. After all, what makes a mystery story? I would argue that the defining feature of a mystery story is a central puzzle (usually a crime, hence the typical bundling together in bookstores as “mystery/crime”) where the truth is hidden until the end. Mysteries rely on an investigator of some kind as a key protagonist, as well as misdirects, suspicions, clues, all of which let the reader follow along with the protagonist until a final reveal.

Given that, it’s easy to see how Contact, and many other First Contact novels like Rendezvous With Rama, The Three-Body Problem, Semiosis, Solaris, The Mountain In The Sea, and even my own new novel The Fist Of Memory, function on a significant level, as mystery stories. The puzzle may have shifted from a murder in a locked room to an alien signal/presence, but the narrative engine is the same: evidence appears, theories emerge, assumptions are challenged, and the truth slowly reveals itself.

That last bit is important. Both First contact stories and mystery fiction depend on information asymmetry and management to be effective. In both cases, truth emerges in fragments, until a final big reveal which should be both surprising and make complete sense in hindsight.

A mystery where the investigator reveals the solution too soon or without sufficient buildup can be unsatisfying. First Contact narratives are pretty much the same. They derive their emotional and philosophical power from a series of carefully managed revelations.

A perfect example is the movie Arrival (another one of my favorites) based on the novella “Story of Your Life” by Ted Chiang, in which a linguistics professor Dr. Louise Banks, is recruited by the military to try to communicate with twelve massive alien spacecraft that have landed across Earth to learn why before panicked world governments ignite a global war.

After several false starts and apparent failures, the film’s climax arrives (ha!) in a powerful revelatory moment when she finally comprehends the alien language and her perception of time shifts, as does the audience’s understanding of the film’s events. It’s so brilliantly done; I get chills just thinking about it.

When I started writing my own First Contact SF thriller, The Fist Of Memory, I brought with me that imbibed spirit of mystery as an essential element and I wanted to give readers those familiar feelings. I open the book with a classic first-contact mystery premise, riffing on Rendezvous With Rama (yet another favorite of mine): an enormous alien spacecraft appears in the sky, approaching Earth. It’s uncommunicative and unresponsive to our signals.

My main character Tope is an assassin caught in the very Nigerian brand of political turmoil the alien craft’s arrival precipitates (inspired by my experience growing up under political instability). But once I had that opening as my setup, I knew I also needed a scientist as one of my protagonists. Because in First Contact, the scientists and explorers perform the same role that detectives perform in mystery and crime fiction: discover something previously unknown, gather evidence, analyze clues, formulate hypotheses, eliminate suspicions, search for patterns, solve the puzzle.

So, I created Itumeleng Sefako, an astronomer struggling to balance his scientific beliefs and his cultural traditions and connections. It’s through him that the mystery of aliens as well as their connection between humanity is investigated, analyzed and eventually revealed. Tope and Itumeleng become co-protagonists, performing a literary pas de deux, but without Itumeleng working through the core mystery, the book wouldn’t work.

That said, I think there is one thing that First Contact stories can do which traditional mysteries and detective fiction cannot (at least not without risking the ire of readers) and that’s this: leave the mystery unsolved (as is the case in Rendezvous With Rama). First Contact stories can do this because a truly alien intelligence may lie beyond our capacity for understanding. Or their worldview may be so radically different from ours that it’s essentially incomprehensible.

Think of all the meetings of separate human cultures/civilizations that were previously unaware of each other and just how many misunderstandings there were. Now increase that several orders of magnitude. Can we ever understand the motivations of, say, boron-based sentient crystals? Could we comprehend the morality of an inorganic mind that evolved in the magnetic poles of a neutron star? Sometimes, in First Contact, the closer we approach a solution, the more we discover the limits of our own perception.

Luckily, like in Contact, I chose not to lean into this too much in The Fist Of Memory. The mystery is resolved. At the end of the novel, there is an explanation of who/what the aliens are and a reveal that leaves all of humanity with a choice and a potential for change.

I felt this was important because in the end, while First Contact stories are ostensibly about humans meeting the other, they aren’t really about that. Not really. They’re about us. They’re a storytelling device through which we examine ourselves, attempting to think through the mystery of who we are and what our place in the universe might be.

Ultimately, First Contact stories are really mystery stories because they are driven by our own endless search for meaning and that, I think, is what makes them so appealing.

Wole Talabi is an engineer, writer, and editor from Nigeria. He is the author of the critically acclaimed Shigidi And The Brass Head Of Obalufon, which was named one of the best books of 2023 by The Washington Post, as well as The Fist of Memory. He has hopped around the planet quite a bit but right now lives in Australia. He has been a finalist for the Hugo, Nebula and Locus awards, the Caine Prize, and has won the Sidewise award for alternate history. Talabi's work has also been translated into 7 languages. His fiction has appeared in Asimov's, F&SF, Clarkesworld, and is collected in the books Incomplete Solutions (2019, Luna Press) and Convergence Problems (2024, DAW Books).

#7742. Court declines to restore Biden-era regulation allowing some deportation proceedings to be suspended

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to restore a Biden-era regulation that allows immigration judges to suspend some deportation proceedings. In a brief, unsigned order, the court turned down a request from three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants to pause an agreement between Texas and the U.S. Department of Justice that threw out the rule.

The regulation at the center of the dispute, which provides what is known as “administrative closure,” was adopted by the Executive Office for Immigration Review, part of the Department of Justice, in 2024. Under it, immigration judges may suspend some deportation proceedings – for example, to allow a crime victim or witness to seek relief, such as asylum, from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which is a separate agency.

In June of this year, Texas went to federal court in Wichita Falls, where its case was assigned to Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor – the only federal judge in that area. Calling the administrative-closure rule “one part of the Biden-Harris Administration’s campaign to undermine our immigration laws,” it alleged that the EOIR does not have the authority to adopt the administrative-closure rule. Instead, it wrote, federal law requires an immigration judge, at the end of a proceeding, to “decide whether an alien is removable from the United States.”

Just a few hours after the case was filed, the DOJ and Texas asked O’Connor to enter a final judgment for the state. The DOJ also asked him both to throw out the rule altogether and to issue an order making clear that the EOIR could not adopt a similar rule in the future. O’Connor granted those requests on the same day.

On Aug. 7, three cities with large immigrant populations – Baltimore, Maryland; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio – and Centro Legal de la Raza, which provides legal services to immigrants, filed an emergency motion to join the case so that they could defend the administrative-closure rule on appeal, when neither Texas nor the federal government intended to do so. O’Connor denied their request on the ground that they lacked a legal right to sue, known as standing. In particular, he rejected the cities’ contention that the elimination of the rule would cost them money because their taxpayers are likely to be deported.

The challengers then went to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, which rejected their request to block the consent judgment between Texas and the Department of Justice and thereby reinstate the administrative-closure rule while their appeal continued.

On Oct. 9, the challengers came to the Supreme Court, calling the consent agreement the product of “egregious collusion” and asking the justices to step in. Their attorney, Joshua Salzman of Democracy Forward, argued that permitting the consent agreement to stand could have widespread implications. “If a judgment procured through such open collusion is allowed to remain in effect,” he wrote, “any agency can avoid the strictures of the” federal law governing administrative agencies “by advertising its unwillingness to defend a disfavored regulation and by immediately acquiescing to nationwide relief.”

Urging the Supreme Court to leave the agreement in place, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer contended that the challengers’ request to pause O’Connor’s ruling “attempts to improperly leverage a clear-cut dispute over” the challengers’ efforts to join the case “into a far-reaching attack on the merits of” the court’s approval of the agreement. For its part, Texas told the justices that putting O’Connor’s ruling on hold “would revive a rule the district court declared unlawful, renew the fiscal and sovereign injuries Texas alleged, and unsettle a final judgment accepted by the actual parties.”

Four days after the case was fully briefed, the court denied the challengers’ request without comment.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7741. Crime and the city: Harbin, China

Harbin, capital of China’s Heilongjiang Province—what used to be known as Manchuria—China’s “Wild East.” It’s long been China’s most northerly and Russified city—train lines into Russia and for many decades run by the Russians to the warm-water port of Dalian and connecting to the Trans-Siberian Railway. And then, after 1917, a new Russian influx fleeing the Bolsheviks.

Even today, sitting up towards the border at the Amur River between China and Russia’s vast Far Eastern provinces, the city has onion dome Orthodox churches and synagogues with streets that would not look out of place Khabarovsk or Tomsk. But this is certainly Chinese territory now and so crime writing is, as we’ve seen in Crime and the City columns on Shanghai, Beijing and Chengdu subject to certain censorship and restrictions.

Yangsze Choo’s The Fox Wife (2024) is set up in Manchuria in 1908 where young woman is found frozen in the snow. Her death is clouded by rumors of fox spirits, believed to lure people into peril by transforming into beautiful women and men. Bao, a detective with a reputation for sniffing out the truth, is hired to uncover the dead woman’s identity. Since childhood, Bao has been intrigued by the fox gods, yet they’ve remained tantalizingly out of reach. Until, perhaps, now.

American Sinologist Scott Seligman’s true crime Murder in Manchuria (2023) is a brilliant evocation of the Soviet spies and fascists, adventurers and chancers who gathered in interwar Harbin, a city at once highly modern—trains, art deco hotels, American cars—yet with old world animosities that boil over into kidnapping, murder and espionage.

Semyon Kaspé, a young Jewish musician, is kidnapped, tortured, and ultimately murdered by disaffected, antisemitic White Russians, secretly acting on the orders of Japanese military overlords who covet his father’s wealth. When local authorities deliberately slow-walk the search for the kidnappers, a young French diplomat takes over and launches his own investigation. Amazing…. And it’s all true!

Novelist Mark Oulton fictionalizes this same period in Red Spy in Harbin 1: In the Making (2025). It’s 1935 Harbin, a city of spies, racketeers, and would-be revolutionaries. Chinese agent Chen Minghe is ordered to infiltrate the Russian émigré Fascist Party—led by Konstantin Rodzaevsky, a real-life White émigré whose vanity and erratic leadership belie his dangerous ambitions. 1937 dawns and full-scale war with Japan begins, Chen’s mission starts to unravel. Rodzaevsky’s affair with a planted mistress comes to light. The resulting scandal begins to unravel the operation.

Chen’s adventures in espionage continue in Red Spy in Harbin: Book 2: The Price of Survival (2026) but in this tale move to World War Two Japanese occupied Taiwan.

Another series with Harbin at its centre and in the same “nest of spies” interwar period is Tom Stickel’s Special District: Harbin: Drawing the Tiger’s Bones (2022). It’s 1929 A patrolman, Borya Melnikov, sits at the bottom ranks of Harbin’s Special District police force. A dismembered body. A raging Red Terror campaign. A brewing war with the Soviet Union….Borya is assigned to investigate the dismembered body of one the city’s foreign businessmen uncovered in the nearby Japanese zone.

Special District: Harbin: Book 2: The Tigers of East Mountain (2023) starts with the discovery of body of a local Jewish businessman in a Harbin back alley threatens to tip the city into mob violence… It’s 1932 and Borya Melnikov returns to police ranks after the Japanese take over Harbin and end Soviet control, only this time with the Judicial Police of the new state of Manchukuo (Japanese- occupied Manchuria).

And finally, Special District: Harbin: Book 3: Visiting the Tiger’s Den (2024). It’s 1935, and Borya Melnikov has risen to the rank of Senior Inspector on Harbin’s Judicial Police unit in Manchuria. But his position is becoming untenable as Manchukuo’s Japanese masters are increasingly intolerant of his independent style…and now this anonymous threat lands on his desk. It’s not in his nature to back down to threats, but it is only weeks before his wife returns to Harbin. He must quickly solve all four of his open investigations before she arrives or risk putting her into danger also.

Brian Klingborg’s City of Ice (2021) is more contemporary and has Harbin partially as a backdrop. In a remote Chinese town – where the theft of a few chickens counts as a major crime—a young woman is found brutally murdered…with her heart, lungs and liver removed.

Inspector Lu Fei, a weary cop who fled the city, suddenly finds himself under the intense scrutiny of the ruling party in Beijing. Determined to find her killer, Lu Fei must navigate a society where politics can be deadly, corruption is rife, and the powerful are untouchable. As evidence connects the case to a string of unsolved murders, Lu must decide what he will risk in search of justice….

There are more Lu Fei novels, mostly set in northern China, including Thief of Souls (2021), The Magistrate (2023) and Wild Prey (2022), which takes Lu Fei to Myanmar.

Caroline Petit has written several historical fictions set in China, usually southern China—Hong Kong and Macao. The Fat Man’s Daughter (2006) ranges too from Hong Kong up to Manchuria. In Hong Kong in 1937 orphan 19-year-old Leah Kolbe is approached by a Mr. Chang, who claims to have known her father and offers her a commission to go to Manchukuo to smuggle out Chinese Imperial treasures. She consents and, accompanied by her faithful amah and a Russian émigré woman in Chang’s pay, takes the train north.

And finally, a writer I’ve been trying to squeeze into Crime and the City for a long time, Japanese author Haruki Murakami. Not naturally a crime writer admittedly but his novel The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle (1994) counts I reckon. Toru Okada, an unemployed man living a quiet suburban life in Tokyo, watches his life unravel after his cat disappears, his wife Kumiko grows increasingly distant, and he starts receiving strange phone calls.

From there the story explores deep psychological trauma, historical violence (particularly Japan’s actions in World War Two in Manchuria), personal alienation, and the hidden depths of human memory. The Manchurian sections of the novel are extremely atmospheric and often harrowing, a stark, visceral departure from his usual dreamlike, whimsical magical realism.

It is a book partly about Japan’s war crimes in China, brutality and multi-generational trauma. A trauma, by the way, that still lingers over Heilongjiang Province and the city of Harbin.

Paul French is a British author of books about modern Chinese history and contemporary Chinese society including Midnight in Peking and the 2018 release City of Devils.

#7738. Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.

Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.

“Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

“For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”

“Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States.”

“Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” said Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.”

According to court documents, Lemma held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance. From 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, Lemma conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States.

Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government.

During his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings.

Specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked.

On some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].”

According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. If accepted by the court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. Sentencing is set for April 14, 2027.

The investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office.

The matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division.

#7737. ‘Judge Stone’ by Viola Davis and James Patterson wins inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Legal Fiction

Viola Davis (left) and James Patterson appeared in New York City in March for a discussion of their book, “Judge Stone,” which was chosen as the winner of the inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Excellence in Legal Fiction. (Photo by Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images)

Judge Stone, by acclaimed actor Viola Davis and prolific author James Patterson, has been chosen as the winner of the inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Excellence in Legal Fiction.

The prize, which is being awarded by the ABA Journal, the University of Miami School of Law and the University of Miami College of Arts & Sciences, was determined by a panel of judges that featured former ABA Presidents Deborah Enix-Ross and Carolyn Lamm, California Court of Appeal Justice Lee Smalley Edmon and Turow himself.

A public poll hosted by the ABA Journal also chose Judge Stone as the favorite for the prize from among the field of three finalists, which also included A Pair of Aces by Marie Benedict and Victoria Christopher Murray, and Grave Danger by James Grippando.

The Turow Prize aims to honor the work that best illuminates the role of lawyers in society and their power to effect meaningful change. It is a successor to the prestigious Harper Lee Prize, which the Journal and the University of Alabama previously awarded to outstanding works of legal fiction, including novels by John Grisham, Michael Connelly and Grippando.

Judge Stone is a legal thriller about a Black woman judge from a small town in Alabama who presides over a controversial case. It is the first collaboration between Davis and Patterson.

Davis is one of a select group of celebrities who are “EGOT” winners for taking home Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony awards. In 2025, she was honored by the Golden Globes with the Cecil B. DeMille Award for “outstanding contributions to the world of entertainment.”

She won an Emmy for TV’s How to Get Away with Murder and has appeared in numerous films, including Academy Award–nominated Doubt, The Help and Fences (for which she received the Oscar). She won two Tonys (for Fences and King Hedley II) and a Grammy for best audiobook, narration and storytelling recording for her memoir, Finding Me. She also took home a Screen Actors Guild Award for her role in Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom.

In his long career, Patterson has created notable characters and series including Alex Cross, the Women’s Murder Club, Jane Smith and Maximum Ride. He’s written true stories about the Kennedys, John Lennon and Tiger Woods, and has coauthored No. 1 bestselling novels with Bill Clinton, Dolly Parton and Michael Crichton. He’s received an Edgar Award, ten Emmy Awards, the Literarian Award from the National Book Foundation and the National Humanities Medal, according to jamespatterson.com.

Named in honor of pioneering attorney and international bestselling author Scott Turow—the “father of the modern legal thriller”—the Turow Prize seeks to unearth compelling works of fiction that illuminate the dynamics of law, the justice system and the human experience.

Turow’s 13 fiction and two nonfiction books, including Presumed Innocent and the current Presumed Guilty, have sold over 30 million copies worldwide and been adapted for film and television.

Davis and Patterson will receive a cash prize and a signed copy of Presumed Innocent at the award ceremony and reception on Nov. 19 hosted by the University of Miami, along with the exclusive right to feature the prestigious Turow Prize logo on their winning book’s cover.

#7733. Two cheers for “insecure originalism”

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In his new book, Justice Samuel Alito takes aim at what he calls judicial “insecurity,” or a judge’s self-conscious worry that he might be advancing his own policy preferences under the guise of impartial adjudication. “Twenty-first century originalists,” he argues, “should shed this insecure mindset.”

Alito’s suggestion is at odds with decades of conservative legal thought, including remarks by Justice Antonin Scalia. More fundamentally, what Alito labels insecurity is better understood as a form of humility and self-awareness. And that humility is laudable for all judges, not just originalists. There is much more to fear from the self-assured or overconfident judge than the insecure one.

In some of the book’s most discussed passages (and in an op-ed in The Wall Street Journal), Alito impugns “insecure originalism,” in part because “insecurity” may lead originalists “to worry that they are subconsciously engaging in ‘results-oriented’ decision-making and ‘judicial activism’ in the service of their own policy preferences.” Alito urges originalists to shrug off this worry: “Originalist judges should . . . be on guard against subconsciously setting a higher bar for legal arguments that yield outcomes they find desirable as a policy matter.”

The insecurity that Alito bemoans has a rich history that his discussion omits. In recent decades, the jurist most associated with this kind of thinking was longtime conservative hero Scalia. In his oft-repeated view, “The judge who always likes the results he reaches is a bad judge.” This maxim was admonitory. It not so subtly suggested that other judges, perhaps of the non-originalist variety, always liked where their theorizing led them. But not the principled originalist, whose impartial theory necessarily brought about disappointment – the price of integrity.

Scalia often fleshed out this line of thinking by pointing to specific issues that originalism resolved in ways he claimed to find regrettable. The First Amendment, in Scalia’s view, encompassed a right to burn the American flag, something that Scalia personally found distasteful. And the confrontation clause effectively demanded that many serious offenders go unpunished. Scalia’s critics sometimes chafed when he drew attention to these decisions, which seemed to give him permission to issue other rulings that did align with his own policy preferences.

Scalia’s disciples have long echoed his view of the “bad judge.” In published writings, including a judicial opinion, Justice Neil Gorsuch has favorably adapted Scalia’s “bad judge” admonition. And Justice Amy Coney Barrett made Scalia’s aphorism a prominent part of her recent memoir and related book tour. Barrett has also offered her own variations on this theme, remarking for instance: “You should sometimes be reaching results that you really dislike.” In a similar spirit, a majority opinion by Justice Brett Kavanaugh defended its own impartiality by adducing examples of standing decisions that cut in different ideological directions.

What Alito labels “insecurity” is really a judicial virtue and better characterized as a form of self-consciousness or rigor. When a judge realizes that he is consistently ruling for or against a particular kind of party, he has good reason to reflect on the possibility that he is the victim of his own biases. That point has special salience in today’s United States, which is marked by partisan polarization.

When a judge confronts a case with partisan valence, he would do well to pause over his own potential bias. In the context of contemporary federal judging, such a bias often correlates with the judge’s appointing president. A judge appointed by a Republican or Democratic president is likely to have personal views aligned with Republicans or Democrats, respectively. And the judge is likely to have a social set that is ideologically skewed. As Alito noted in an interview, such a skew may not be the judge’s doing, so much as the result of ideological backlash against the judge’s rulings. But even if unfair or unfortunate, the backlash’s effects are real.

In this context, a judge will be tempted to please his own ideological tribe while being insensitive to its rival. A Democratic-appointed judge may play to Bluesky, writing zingers in trendy language that please imagined audiences. Or a Republican-appointed judge may similarly look forward to standing ovations at Federalist Society galas. These incentives and trains of thought are not so hypothetical. And once this kind of behavior takes hold, the judges in question become more like partisan actors than principled defenders of either legal rules or the judiciary.

Against that backdrop, an anti-partisanship principle offers a means of reaching better, more accurate results – not a means of sacrificing accuracy for illicit ends. A judge who sensibly factors in his own partisan affiliation, background, or associations is more likely to identify and apply the law by his own lights. Or so one might hope. Whether anti-partisanship can work largely depends on how it is implemented.

There are many ways of implementing anti-partisanship, and different approaches may befit different scenarios or appeal to different jurists. Surely no judge should factor in party identity in a way that squarely contradicts the law’s dictates. And because many judges have sincere legal views with an ideological valence, complete anti-partisanship is both infeasible and undesirable. Yet judging often involves subtle choices. And those subtleties create room for the anti-partisanship principle to have meaningful effect.

At the Supreme Court, certiorari, that is, deciding what case to hear, affords perhaps the most immediate opportunity for discretionary judgments. Is a particular case or issue ripe for prompt consideration, or sufficiently worthy of the court’s attention? These questions yield judgment calls, and a judge may reasonably consider whether he is consistently making these decisions in favor of one party or ideology. Cert might be warranted only when a relatively objective test is satisfied, such as a deep circuit split. Or the justice might have a practice of avoiding expedited review in such cases.

Moreover, all appellate courts confront myriad opportunities to craft the scope and depth of their holdings. A judge who supports one broad holding after another in favor of his appointing president or party is probably ruling irresponsibly. That judge is not merely transgressing principles of minimalism (deciding only what needs to be decided) or gradualism (deciding incrementally) but doing so in an especially objectionable way by ruling grandly with partisan effect. By contrast, a humbler judge will be sure to wait beyond the first or second chance to resolve a major issue when that issue has a partisan valence.

Judges of all kinds also face an array of different grounds on which to rule. An anti-partisan judge might look with care at jurisdictional requirements or opportunities for abstention, adapting Alexander Bickel’s “passive virtues” (that is, pursuing an impassive strategy, rather than ruling either swiftly or grandly). Or he might shelve a holding in the alternative where a single, narrower holding would suffice.

Precedent affords additional opportunities for anti-partisanship. When a party seeks to overrule case law, a judge might ask whether that request has a partisan valence – and then look to see whether the request to overrule has broad, cross-ideological support.

Finally, judges may express themselves differently depending on the presence of partisan tensions. Barrett made this point in Trump v. Anderson, which (as to result) unanimously held that Colorado could not exclude then-candidate Trump from the presidential ballot based on section 3 of the 14th Amendment. She wrote separately to note that the court “has settled a politically charged issue in the volatile season of a Presidential election” and that, “[p]articularly in this circumstance, writings on the Court should turn the national temperature down, not up.” Thus, Anderson was “not the time to amplify disagreement with stridency.” In other contexts, judges may follow this general advice by muting their rhetoric or even suppressing dissents.

In our current polarized environment, it may be hard to imagine that a judge would be too anti-partisan. Yet Alito quite properly raises just that concern.

As Alito insightfully puts it: “insecure originalists may actually welcome occasions when their originalist analysis leads to results they dislike. When that occurs, they experience a gratifying frisson, a brief catharsis in which their anxiety about having unconsciously succumbed to the temptation of results-oriented decision-making is released.” The image here is of a judge who becomes so excited about proving his own impartiality that he becomes utterly partial.

Once again, Alito’s point is hardly limited to originalists, and other commentators have raised similar concerns about judging in general. For example, Judge Richard Posner once noted that “[i]t is a source of satisfaction to a judge to vote for the litigant who irritates him . . . for it is by doing such things that you know that you are playing the judge role.”

This kind of concern shows that the anti-partisanship principle must itself be deployed reflectively and cautiously. There is no one simple trick for impartial or accurate judging, and any maxim of juridical wisdom can be twisted or taken too much to heart.

Alito’s worry also indicates that the anti-partisanship principle has only contingent appeal. In a less polarized polity, partisanship might play a smaller or even a trivial role in judicial decision-making. In that environment, the anti-partisanship principle would not help – or might even worsen – judicial bias. But that is not our world today.

Alito elaborates his point in a way that further underscores the appeal of anti-partisanship. To wit, he notes that “an originalist judge should not cavalierly or happily embrace results that defy common sense.” Attention to common sense is indeed justifiable, but that is because (or if) it is truly “common.” Consensus views may well provide a helpful indication that a particular ruling is senseless, catastrophic, or absurd.

But “common sense” is not at all the same as Alito’s other and more salient subject – namely, “outcomes [judges] find desirable as a policy matter.” In placing these two ideas in successive paragraphs and casting them as comparable, Alito inadvertently reveals how easy it is for a judge to draw an equivalence between, or fail to differentiate, his own highly contestable views and genuine consensus.

Anti-partisanship may not be for everyone. The legal system may even benefit from having some judges in each court who align with one or the other of the nation’s two political parties. That arrangement would help partisans identify with the judiciary and might foster a kind of adversarial system within the third branch. But that picture seems appealing, if at all, only if the partisan judges remain the exception.

In a later chapter, Alito praises Judge Learned Hand’s famous speech on “the Spirit of Liberty.” Alito notes for instance: “I am convinced that the spirit of the Constitution—of limited but effective government, individual rights, and equal justice under law—is alive and well in the hearts of the American people.”

Alas, Alito’s discussion does not quote or acknowledge what Hand believed the spirit of liberty to be. In the speech’s most memorable and oft-repeated line, Hand posited: “The spirit of liberty is the spirit which is not too sure that it is right.”

One might say that the spirit of liberty is a bit insecure. The spirit of the Constitution is, too.

Richard M. Re is a professor at Harvard Law School. Early in his career, he clerked for then-Judge Brett M. Kavanaugh and Justice Anthony M. Kennedy.

#7730. Wells Fargo faces labor board complaint over union vote

The National Labor Relations Board alleged the lender threatened and retaliated against workers in favor of unionization at a California branch.

The National Labor Relations Board has accused Wells Fargo of illegally threatening and retaliating against employees and coercing workers to prevent fair unionization votes at a California branch.

Most employees of an Atwater, California, branch who signed cards supporting unionization in December 2023 voted against unionization the following month, a regional director of the NLRB alleged, in a complaint filed Feb. 11 and seen by Bloomberg,

The NLRB claims Wells Fargo coerced workers to vote against unionization. Wells Fargo has denied that allegation.

The labor board wants the bank to recognize and negotiate with the union despite the vote, based on a 2023 precedent case. The 2023 Cemex ruling strengthened the NLRB's power to compel companies that violate labor laws to recognize unions.

However, Republicans and business groups oppose the precedent. The acting general counsel of NLRB, William Cowen, or his permanent replacement, could withdraw, amend, or settle the Wells Fargo complaint.

President Donald Trump appointed Cowen acting general counsel this month, days after firing NLRB’s previous chief lawyer Jennifer Abruzzo, a Biden appointee, and Democratic board member Gwynne Wilcox.

The email notifying Wilcox of her termination said she was being fired since she did not “share the objectives” of the present administration. Wilcox’s ouster has left the board with only two members coupled with existing vacancies and does not meet the minimum number of members needed to adjudicate routine cases.

Wilcox is suing Trump, alleging the president surpassed his authority in firing her and requesting that she be allowed to resume her work as an NLRB member.

The NLRB complaint does not signify a complete investigation or a full adjudication of the allegations; rather, the regional office found that the allegations may be sufficient to go to a hearing to consider all evidence and make credibility determinations, a Wells Fargo spokesperson noted.

Employees at the Atwater branch voted 3-1 to reject unionization in January 2024. The branch manager allegedly told staff she knew about organizing discussions and warned about camera surveillance. She also reportedly told workers that Wells Fargo would apply stricter work conditions and would make union supporters stay longer hours.

A Wells Fargo spokesperson said the bank trains its managers to respect the rights of its employees to freely associate and join or support a union, or to bargain collectively with a representative of their choosing.

“We train our managers to comply with labor law and respect the rights of our employees,” the spokesperson told Banking Dive via email. “In this case, the majority of eligible employees freely voted against a union in a Board supervised secret ballot election and the facts do not support allegations to the contrary.”

Wells Fargo is cooperating with the investigation but believes these allegations are unfounded and plans to defend the company and employees, the spokesperson added.

An NLRB hearing before a judge is scheduled for October, and Wells Fargo, if ordered to collectively bargain, can appeal to NLRB members in Washington, Bloomberg reported.

Recently, unionized Wells Fargo employees hit a new challenge in organizing. The bank's conduct management intake team won its union vote 21-16 in December, making it the first non-branch unit at Wells Fargo to unionize.

The team, which handles customer and employee complaints across various locations, has now filed an unfair labor practice charge with the NLRB through Wells Fargo Workers United-CWA. The complaint alleges that the bank illegally refuses to engage in collective bargaining following the certified union vote, American Banker reported. However, the bank contends it’s waiting for the outcome of the NLRB’s review and claims there were procedural flaws in the handling of the vote.

CWA unionized 24 Wells Fargo branches last year, with around 200 employees being organized.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf pushed back on employee unionization efforts last April, saying it’s important to “make clear that we continue to believe that our employees are best served by working directly with Wells Fargo and our leadership team.”
